text: बायोम धरती का एक बड़ा इलाका है, जहाँ की [[climate|जलवायु]], पौधे और जानवर मिलते-जुलते होते हैं। वर्षावन, रेगिस्तान, घास के मैदान और टुंड्रा, ये सब बायोम हैं।

बायोम को गढ़ने वाली दो सबसे बड़ी चीज़ें हैं तापमान और बारिश। ये दोनों मिलकर तय करते हैं कि कौन-से पौधे उग सकते हैं। फिर पौधे तय करते हैं कि कौन-से जानवर वहाँ रह सकते हैं, क्योंकि जानवरों को खाने और ठिकाने के लिए उनकी ज़रूरत होती है।

बायोम एक जैसी जगहों को एक समूह में रखने का तरीका है, चाहे वे एक-दूसरे से कितनी भी दूर हों। भारत का थार रेगिस्तान और अमेरिका का मोहावी रेगिस्तान दुनिया के आमने-सामने के छोरों पर हैं। फिर भी दोनों रेगिस्तान हैं, जहाँ काँटेदार पौधे हैं और ऐसे जानवर हैं जो लंबे समय तक बिना पानी के रह सकते हैं।

वैज्ञानिक ज़मीन को थोड़े अलग-अलग ढंग से बाँटते हैं, पर ज़्यादातर सूचियों में ये शामिल होते हैं।

जंगल सबसे बड़े बायोमों में से हैं, जो धरती की ज़मीन का लगभग एक तिहाई हिस्सा ढकते हैं। इनमें गरम, नम [[@rainforests|वर्षावन]] हैं, सूखे मौसम या सर्दियों में पत्ते गिराने वाले जंगल हैं, और चीड़ और स्प्रूस के ठंडे उत्तरी जंगल हैं।

[[@grasslands|घास के मैदानों]] में घास के लिए तो काफ़ी बारिश होती है, पर आमतौर पर बहुत-से पेड़ों के लिए नहीं। अफ़्रीका के [[savanna|सवाना]], अमेरिका के ग्रेट प्लेन्स और भारत के अपने घास के मैदान, जैसे गुजरात का बन्नी, इसके उदाहरण हैं।

[[@deserts-sand|रेगिस्तानों]] में बहुत कम बारिश होती है। कुछ गरम हैं, जैसे सहारा और थार। दूसरे, जैसे गोबी और लद्दाख के कुछ हिस्से, ठंडे हैं।

[[@tundra|टुंड्रा]] सुदूर उत्तर में और पहाड़ों की ऊँचाइयों पर पेड़ों से ख़ाली ठंडी ज़मीन है, जहाँ गरमी का मौसम छोटा होता है।

sec.h: जीवन बायोम के हिसाब से ढलता है
sec.t:
हर बायोम में ज़िंदा रहने की अपनी तरकीबें हैं। कैक्टस जैसे रेगिस्तानी पौधे मोटे तनों में पानी जमा करते हैं, और उनमें पत्तियों की जगह काँटे होते हैं। [[@camels|ऊँट]] कई दिन बिना पिए रह सकते हैं।

वर्षावन के पौधे घनी [[canopy|छतरी]] के नीचे रोशनी पकड़ने के लिए बड़ी-बड़ी पत्तियाँ उगाते हैं। घास के मैदानों में बाइसन, ज़ेबरा और काला हिरन जैसे चरने वाले जानवर झुंडों में रहते हैं, कुछ हद तक खुले मैदान में सुरक्षा के लिए।

टुंड्रा में पौधे नीचे-नीचे और छोटे उगते हैं, और आर्कटिक लोमड़ी जैसे जानवरों के मोटे बाल होते हैं। टुंड्रा की बहुत-सी चिड़ियाँ सर्दियों के लिए दक्षिण की ओर उड़ जाती हैं।

{{story:animal-migration-land}}

1802 में जर्मनी के खोजी अलेक्ज़ेंडर फ़ॉन हम्बोल्ट भूमध्य रेखा के पास इक्वाडोर के एक ज्वालामुखी, चिम्बोराज़ो, पर काफ़ी ऊँचाई तक चढ़े। उन्होंने देखा कि चढ़ते-चढ़ते पौधे पट्टियों में बदलते जा रहे थे।

नीचे उष्णकटिबंधीय जंगल थे। ऊपर ठंडे जंगल आए, फिर घास और झाड़ियाँ, फिर काई और लाइकेन, और आख़िर में बर्फ़। कुछ किलोमीटर ऊपर चढ़ने का असर ध्रुवों की ओर हज़ारों किलोमीटर सफ़र करने जैसा था।

हम्बोल्ट ने पहाड़ का एक मशहूर चित्र बनाया, जिसमें पौधों की हर पट्टी पर नाम लिखा था। इससे वैज्ञानिकों को यह समझने में मदद मिली कि जलवायु हर जगह एक जैसे पैटर्न में जीवन को गढ़ती है। हिमालय में भी तुम यही देख सकते हो, तलहटी के साल के जंगलों से लेकर ऊँचे बुग्यालों और नंगी चट्टानों तक।

पानी के भी बायोम होते हैं। मीठे पानी के बायोम में नदियाँ, झीलें और तालाब आते हैं। समुद्री बायोम महासागरों को ढकते हैं, मूँगा चट्टानों से लेकर गहरे समुद्र तक। जहाँ नदियाँ समुद्र से मिलती हैं, वहाँ [[@mangroves|मैंग्रोव]] और आर्द्रभूमि दोनों के बीच ख़ास जगहें बनाते हैं, जैसे पश्चिम बंगाल और बांग्लादेश के तट पर सुंदरबन।

बहुत कम देशों में भारत जितने बायोम हैं। देश भर की एक लंबी यात्रा में तुम लद्दाख के ठंडे रेगिस्तान से पश्चिमी घाट के हरे वर्षावनों तक पहुँच सकते हो। और पूरब में मध्य भारत के घास के मैदान और सुंदरबन के मैंग्रोव हैं।

अमेरिका में भी खूब विविधता है: अलास्का का टुंड्रा, एरिज़ोना के रेगिस्तान, बीच के इलाके के प्रेयरी घास के मैदान, और प्रशांत के उत्तर-पश्चिमी तट के नम जंगल। जैसे-जैसे जलवायु गरम हो रही है, वैज्ञानिक देख रहे हैं कि बायोम की सीमाएँ खिसक रही हैं: पेड़ पहाड़ों पर ऊपर और उत्तर में टुंड्रा की ओर बढ़ रहे हैं, और कुछ सूखी ज़मीनें फैल रही हैं।

text: हाँ, कुछ रेत के टीले सच में गाते हैं। जब कुछ ख़ास टीलों की खड़ी ढलान से सूखी रेत फिसलती है, तो एक गहरी, एक-सी गुनगुनाहट होती है, जैसे सारंगी या चेलो का कोई धीमा सुर, या दूर उड़ते हवाई जहाज़ की घरघराहट। यह आवाज़ कई मिनट चल सकती है और किलोमीटरों दूर तक जा सकती है।

वैज्ञानिकों को दुनिया में लगभग 35 ऐसी जगहें पता हैं जहाँ "गूँजते" या "गाते" टीले हैं, चीन और मोरक्को से लेकर कैलिफ़ोर्निया, चिली और ओमान के रेगिस्तानों तक। हर टीला अपने अलग स्वर में गुनगुनाता है। कुछ इतने ज़ोर से गाते हैं जितना बगल में चलती घास काटने की मशीन।
आवाज़ ख़ुद रेत से आती है। लाखों कण मिलकर एक साफ़ स्वर कैसे गा लेते हैं, इस पर अब भी बहस है।

हर टीला नहीं गाता। रेत बहुत सूखी होनी चाहिए, और कण गोल, चिकने और लगभग एक ही आकार के होने चाहिए, ज़्यादातर सिलिका के बने, वही चीज़ जिससे काँच बनता है। गीली, धूल भरी या नुकीली रेत चुप रहती है। गाते टीले भी बारिश के बाद तब तक चुप रहते हैं, जब तक फिर से सूख न जाएँ।

गाना तब शुरू होता है जब टीले की खड़ी ढलान पर, जिसे स्लिप फ़ेस कहते हैं, रेत का बहाव शुरू होता है। कभी-कभी हवा इसे शुरू करती है। अक्सर सैलानी, ढलान पर फिसलकर। जैसे ही रेत नीचे उमड़ती है, टीला गुनगुनाने लगता है।

स्वर धीमा होता है, आम तौर पर लगभग 70 से 110 [[vibration|कंपन]] प्रति सेकंड के बीच। यह मोटे तौर पर उतना ही है जितने सबसे नीचे के सुर कोई आदमी गा सकता है। इसे तुम कानों से जितना सुनते हो, उतना ही सीने में महसूस करते हो, जैसा [[@sound-travel|आवाज़ कैसे सफ़र करती है]] में समझ सकते हो।

यहाँ वैज्ञानिकों में मतभेद है। फ़्रांस का एक दल, जिसमें स्टेफ़ान दुआदी और ब्रूनो आंद्रेओत्ती हैं, कहता है कि बहाव में कण क़दम से क़दम मिलाकर चलने लगते हैं, ताल में एक-दूसरे से टकराते हुए। हर टक्कर हवा को धकेलती है, और लाखों एक साथ होती टक्करें एक स्वर बनाती हैं, जैसे स्टेडियम में पूरी भीड़ एक साथ ताली बजाए।

कैलिफ़ोर्निया के कैलटेक में मेलानी हंट की अगुवाई वाले दल का विचार अलग है। उन्होंने पाया कि गाते टीलों में अक्सर ऊपर एक सूखी परत होती है, जो नीचे की सख़्त, नम परत पर टिकी होती है। उन्हें लगता है कि ऊपरी परत [[sound|ध्वनि]] की तरंगों को क़ैद करके गुँजा देती है, कुछ-कुछ गिटार के खोखले ढाँचे की तरह।

दोनों दल प्रयोगों में रेत को गुनगुनवा सकते हैं, पर अभी तक कोई भी विचार हर टीले को नहीं समझा पाता।

टीले सिर्फ़ गाते नहीं। उनमें से बहुत-से चलते भी हैं। हवा रेत को टीले की हल्की ढलान से ऊपर उड़ाती है और चोटी के पार स्लिप फ़ेस पर गिरा देती है। कण-कण करके पूरा टीला आगे सरकता है।

छोटे, अर्धचंद्र जैसे टीले, जिन्हें बरख़ान कहते हैं, साल में दसियों मीटर चल सकते हैं। कुछ रेगिस्तानों में चलते टीले सड़कों, रेल लाइनों और गाँवों तक को दबा देते हैं। राजस्थान के [[@thar-formed|थार रेगिस्तान]] में किसान टीलों को अपनी जगह थामे रखने के लिए घास और पेड़ लगाते हैं।

टीले दूसरी दुनियाओं में भी चलते हैं। मंगल की [[orbit|कक्षा]] में घूमते कैमरों ने वहाँ की पतली हवाओं से धकेले गए टीलों को कुछ सालों में खिसकते देखा है।

और सबसे अजीब बात? कैलिफ़ोर्निया की एक सूखी झील की तलहटी में रेत नहीं, भारी चट्टानें चलती हैं। वे ज़मीन पर पीछे लंबी लकीरें छोड़ती हुई सरकती हैं, और यह पहेली 2014 में जाकर सुलझी, जैसा तुम [[@mystery-sailing-stones|सेलिंग स्टोन्स]] में पढ़ सकते हो।

text: [[renewable|Renewable]] energy comes from sources that nature refills quickly, on a human timescale. Sunlight arrives every day. The wind keeps blowing because the Sun heats the Earth unevenly. Rain keeps refilling rivers. Heat keeps leaking out from deep inside the Earth. Plants regrow.

Coal, oil and [[@earth-weird-door-to-hell|natural gas]] are different. They formed from ancient plants and sea creatures over millions of years. Once we burn them, they are gone, and burning them releases [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] that warms the planet.

So no energy source lasts forever, since even the Sun will change in about 5 billion years. But for people, sunlight, wind, water and underground heat will never run out. In 2023, renewables made about 30% of the world's electricity.

st.reveal: Grid batteries store extra power in the day and release it at night. Pumped hydro uses spare electricity to push water uphill into a reservoir, then lets it run back down through turbines when power is needed. Mixing solar with wind and hydro also helps.

sec.t:
The Sun sends Earth far more energy than people could ever use. Roughly an hour and a half of sunlight carries as much energy as all of humanity uses in a year. [[@solar-panels|Solar panels]] turn sunlight straight into electricity, and they have become much cheaper over the past 15 years.

India has some of the world's largest solar parks. Bhadla, in the [[@thar-formed|Thar Desert]] of Rajasthan, spreads panels across an area larger than some cities. Rooftop panels now sit on homes, schools and railway stations. In 2015, the [[@airports|airport]] at [[@kochi|Kochi]] in Kerala began running entirely on solar power.

[[@wind-turbines|Wind turbines]] work best on windy coasts, plains and hills. Tamil Nadu and Gujarat lead in India, while Texas produces more wind power than any other US state.

sec.h: The hard part: when the wind stops
sec.t:
The Sun sets and the wind drops, but people want power all the time. This is the biggest challenge for renewable energy. Engineers solve it in a few ways. They spread solar and wind farms across large areas, since it is rarely calm and cloudy everywhere at once. They build huge [[@batteries-phones|batteries]], similar to the ones in phones but the size of shipping containers. And they use pumped hydro, which stores energy by pumping water uphill and releasing it later.

Some scientists are also working on [[@hydrogen-fuel|hydrogen made with clean electricity]], and on [[@nuclear-fusion|fusion]], which tries to copy the way the Sun makes energy. These are still being developed.

Renewables are not free of problems. Solar parks and wind farms need lots of land. Panels, turbines and batteries need [[@asteroid-mining|metals that must be mined]]. Large dams can drown forests and force villages to move, which has caused protests in India and elsewhere, such as over the Sardar Sarovar dam on the Narmada.

Still, the sunlight, wind and water will keep arriving whatever we decide. Many countries, including India and the USA, are building renewable power quickly, partly to cut the pollution that causes [[@climate-change|climate change]]. India has set a goal of 500 gigawatts of power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030.

text: संयुक्त राष्ट्र की संस्था विश्व मौसम विज्ञान संगठन (WMO) धरती के मौसम की हदों की आधिकारिक सूची रखती है। जानकारों की एक टीम हर दावे को ध्यान से जाँचती है: उपकरण, रजिस्टर, और उस समय का मौसम।

इसकी सूची में हवा का सबसे ऊँचा तापमान 56.7 °C है, जो 10 जुलाई 1913 को अमेरिका के कैलिफ़ोर्निया में [[@mystery-sailing-stones|डेथ वैली]] के फ़र्नेस क्रीक में नापा गया। सबसे कम −89.2 °C है, जो 21 जुलाई 1983 को अंटार्कटिका में रूस के वोस्तोक स्टेशन पर दर्ज हुआ। बारिश के रिकॉर्ड भारत के पास हैं: [[@meghalaya|मेघालय]] का मॉसिनराम औसतन सबसे गीली जगह है, जहाँ साल में लगभग 12 मीटर बारिश होती है।
नई नापें आने और पुरानी दोबारा जाँचे जाने से रिकॉर्ड बदलते रहते हैं। कुछ पर अब भी बहस चलती है।

st.prompt: 2012 में विश्व मौसम विज्ञान संगठन ने लीबिया का 1922 वाला 58 °C का विश्व रिकॉर्ड रद्द कर दिया। क्यों?

options.t: थर्मामीटर पढ़ने वाले आदमी ने उसे ग़लत पढ़ा था

st.reveal: एक अंतरराष्ट्रीय टीम ने पुराना रजिस्टर जाँचा और उसमें कई गड़बड़ियाँ पाईं। नाप लेने वाला नौसिखिया था, एक अनोखा थर्मामीटर इस्तेमाल कर रहा था और शायद पैमाने का ग़लत हिस्सा पढ़ बैठा। रिकॉर्ड वापस अमेरिका की डेथ वैली के नाम चला गया।

myth: चेरापूंजी धरती की सबसे गीली जगह है।
एक साल में सबसे ज़्यादा बारिश (1860–61) का रिकॉर्ड चेरापूंजी के नाम है, पर पास का मॉसिनराम औसतन थोड़ी ज़्यादा बारिश पाता है। दोनों मेघालय में हैं, लगभग 15 किलोमीटर की दूरी पर।

sec.h: सबसे गर्म, और उस पर शक
sec.t:
90 साल तक सबसे गर्म का रिकॉर्ड लीबिया के अल अज़ीज़िया के नाम था: 1922 में 58 °C। 2012 में WMO की एक टीम ने असली नोट्स पढ़े और पाया कि नाप लेने वाले ने शायद अपना थर्मामीटर ग़लत पढ़ा था। रिकॉर्ड रद्द कर दिया गया।

ख़िताब डेथ वैली की 1913 वाली नाप को मिल गया। मौसम के कुछ इतिहासकार उस पर भी शक करते हैं, क्योंकि उस दिन आसपास के स्टेशन काफ़ी ठंडे थे। पर WMO ने उसे हटाया नहीं है। हाल की गर्मियों में डेथ वैली लगभग 54 °C तक पहुँची है, और ये नापें आधुनिक उपकरणों से ली गई थीं।

भारत में अब तक का सबसे ऊँचा दर्ज [[temperature|तापमान]] 51.0 °C है, जो 19 मई 2016 को राजस्थान के फलोदी में नापा गया।

sec.h: जहाँ सबसे ज़्यादा बारिश होती है
sec.t:
[[@wettest-place|मॉसिनराम]] और चेरापूंजी खासी पहाड़ियों के किनारे पर, लगभग 15 किलोमीटर की दूरी पर बसे हैं। बंगाल की खाड़ी से आती नम मानसूनी हवाएँ इन पहाड़ियों से टकराकर ऊपर उठने को मजबूर होती हैं और बेहिसाब बारिश गिराती हैं। मॉसिनराम में औसतन साल में लगभग 11,800 मिलीमीटर बारिश होती है, बरसाती मुंबई से लगभग पाँच गुना।

एक साल में सबसे ज़्यादा बारिश का रिकॉर्ड चेरापूंजी के नाम है: अगस्त 1860 से जुलाई 1861 के बीच 26 मीटर से ज़्यादा। एक दिन का रिकॉर्ड हिंद महासागर के रेयूनियन द्वीप के पास है। जनवरी 1966 में एक [[cyclone|चक्रवात]] ने वहाँ 24 घंटे में 1,825 मिलीमीटर पानी गिरा दिया, इतना कि एक लंबे-चौड़े आदमी के सिर तक पहुँच जाए।

दूसरी हद पर, चिली के [[@extreme-driest|अटाकामा रेगिस्तान]] के कुछ हिस्सों में लगभग कोई बारिश नहीं होती। कुछ क़स्बों में साल का औसत 1 मिलीमीटर से भी कम है।

[[@tornadoes|बवंडरों]] के अंदर को छोड़ दें, तो [[@extreme-windiest|अब तक नापा गया सबसे तेज़ हवा का झोंका]] 408 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे का था। यह 1996 में उष्णकटिबंधीय चक्रवात ओलिविया के दौरान पश्चिमी ऑस्ट्रेलिया के पास बैरो द्वीप पर आया था।

ओलों के भी रिकॉर्ड हैं। अब तक का सबसे भारी ओला 14 अप्रैल 1986 को बांग्लादेश के गोपालगंज में गिरा, जिसका वज़न लगभग 1 किलो था। सबसे चौड़ा ओला 2010 में साउथ डकोटा के विवियन में मिला, जो 20 सेंटीमीटर चौड़ा था, मोटे तौर पर वॉलीबॉल जितना। [[@hailstorms-india|ऐसे ओले]] तब [[@snow-hail|बनते हैं]], जब गरज वाले बादल में तेज़ ऊपर उठती हवाएँ बर्फ़ को बार-बार ऊपर-नीचे ले जाती हैं और हर बार एक नई परत चढ़ जाती है।

text: Asteroids are leftover building blocks from when the planets formed.

Most live in the [[asteroidbelt|asteroid belt]] between Mars and [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]]. There are well over a million known, from Ceres, about 940 km across, down to boulders the size of a house. Many more are too small to have been spotted.
Jupiter's [[gravity|gravity]] sometimes nudges asteroids into new [[orbit|orbits]], and a few end up crossing Earth's path.

spots: Everything here orbits the Sun. About 4.6 billion years ago, the planets formed from a disc of dust and rock around it.
Our home. Some asteroids cross Earth's path. Scientists watch these closely.
The red planet. Just beyond it lies the asteroid belt.
Millions of rocky leftovers that never became a planet. They're far apart. Spacecraft fly through easily.
The biggest planet. Its strong gravity tugs on asteroids and can nudge some into new paths.

options.t: Probably none at all

quiz.reveal: The belt is enormous, and the asteroids in it are usually hundreds of thousands of kilometres apart. NASA has sent many spacecraft through it without any danger. Visiting an asteroid on purpose takes careful aiming.

This was a popular idea in the 1800s, but the belt doesn't hold nearly enough material to have made a planet. Asteroids are leftovers that never came together into a planet at all.
facts: Total mass of the main belt
about 3 per cent of the Moon's

sec.t:
About 4.6 billion years ago, dust and rock around the young Sun clumped together into planets. Grains stuck together into pebbles, pebbles into boulders, and boulders into small worlds that crashed and merged.

Near Jupiter, its [[gravity|gravity]] stirred things up too much for a planet to form, so the pieces stayed as asteroids. Instead of gently sticking together, they smashed into each other at high speed and broke apart. Over billions of years, Jupiter also flung many of them out of the belt altogether. What remains today is a small fraction of what was once there.

That makes asteroids time capsules. Some have barely changed since the [[solar-system|solar system]] formed, which is how scientists use [[meteorite|meteorites]], pieces of asteroids that fall to Earth, to measure [[@earth-age|Earth's age]].

{{story:earth-age}}

In films, spaceships weave through asteroid belts packed with tumbling rocks. The real belt is nothing like that. Spread the asteroids out over the huge doughnut-shaped region between Mars and Jupiter, and there are usually hundreds of thousands of kilometres between neighbours. Standing on one asteroid, you would probably not see another with your bare eyes.

Put every asteroid in the main belt together and you would get a ball smaller than our Moon, with only about 3 per cent of its mass. Ceres alone makes up about a third of that.

The belt also has gaps. In 1866 the American [[astronomer|astronomer]] Daniel Kirkwood noticed that almost no asteroids orbit at certain distances. Those are places where Jupiter's regular tugs, repeated orbit after orbit, push any asteroid out of its path. They are now called Kirkwood gaps.

sec.h: A planet that turned out to be an asteroid
sec.t:
On 1 January 1801, the Italian astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi, working in Palermo, spotted a faint moving point between Mars and Jupiter. He named it Ceres, after the Roman goddess of farming. For a while it was called a planet. Then astronomers found more objects nearby, and then more again, and a new word was used: asteroid, meaning "star-like".

In 2006, Ceres was [[@dwarf-planets|reclassified as a dwarf planet]], the same decision that changed the status of [[@pluto|Pluto]].

Spacecraft have landed on asteroids and even brought samples back to Earth, so scientists can study the oldest material in the solar system.

Japan's Hayabusa brought back grains from the asteroid Itokawa in 2010, and Hayabusa2 returned samples from Ryugu in 2020. NASA's OSIRIS-REx dropped off a capsule from the asteroid Bennu in September 2023. Inside the Bennu sample, scientists found water-bearing minerals and some of the chemical building blocks of life, such as amino [[acid|acids]]. NASA's Dawn spacecraft orbited both Ceres and the large asteroid Vesta.

Telescopes search every night for asteroids that come near Earth. [[@asteroid-today|Could one hit us?]] and [[@dart|could we push one away?]]

A big one [[@what-if-dinos-lived|did hit Earth 66 million years ago]], helping end the age of the dinosaurs.

text: Most scientists think life could exist on Earth without the Moon. Living things probably appeared in the oceans, and the Sun alone would still give warmth, light and small tides. But the Moon has shaped our planet in deep ways. It makes strong tides, it has slowed Earth's spin, and it may help keep Earth's tilt, and so its seasons, steady.
Without it, life would almost certainly have developed differently. How differently is something scientists still argue about.

st.prompt: If Earth had no Moon, what would happen to ocean tides?

options.t: They would be much smaller, caused only by the Sun
There would be no tides at all
They would be twice as big

st.reveal: The Sun also pulls on the oceans, so there would still be tides. But the Moon causes about two-thirds of today's tides, so they would be roughly a third as big as now.

n.certNote: Life could probably exist without the Moon, but scientists disagree about how different it would be. Early studies said Earth's tilt would swing wildly without the Moon. Later computer models suggest the swings would be smaller and slower than first thought.

Then check a calendar for the Moon's phase. You should see high tides get later by roughly 50 minutes each day, and the biggest tides near full and new moon.
myth: The Moon's pull is strong enough to raise tides in a cup of tea or in our bodies.

sec.h: Tides and the edge of the sea

sec.t:
Earth is tilted on its [[axis|axis]] by about 23.4°. That tilt is why we have [[@seasons-why|seasons]]. The planets, especially Jupiter, tug on Earth and try to change its tilt. The Moon's pull on Earth's bulging middle helps resist this, so the tilt only wobbles between about 22° and 24.5° over tens of thousands of years.

In the 1990s, French scientists calculated that without the Moon, Earth's tilt could swing hugely and unpredictably, perhaps flipping between almost upright and lying on its side. That would make [[climate|climates]] change wildly. But in 2012, American researchers ran new models. They found that a moonless Earth's tilt would still change, but mostly within a narrower range and over very long times. So the Moon helps, but it may not be essential.

Tides also act like a brake. The moving bulges of water rub against the seabed and slowly slow Earth's spin. About 1.4 billion years ago, a day may have lasted only about 18 hours. Soon after [[@moon-formed|the Moon formed]], probably in a giant crash about 4.5 billion years ago, days were shorter still. As Earth slows, the Moon gains energy and drifts outward, about 3.8 cm a year.

In 1963, the scientist John Wells counted tiny daily growth lines on [[fossil|fossil]] corals about 400 million years old. They suggested there were around 400 days in a year back then, because each day was only about 22 hours long. The year was the same length. The days were shorter.

Many animals time their lives by the Moon. On Australia's Great Barrier Reef, many corals release their eggs and sperm together a few nights after a full moon in late spring, in one of the biggest spawning events on Earth. In California, small fish called grunion wriggle onto beaches to lay eggs just after the highest tides, which follow full and new moons.

Many night animals use moonlight to find food or avoid [[predator|predators]]. A world without the Moon would have darker nights, smaller tides, faster days and perhaps a less steady climate. Life would probably still be here, but the [[rhythm|rhythms]] of the shore, the reef and the night would be very different.

text: Air traffic controllers keep planes apart by giving each one its own slice of sky. They watch every plane on radar screens and talk to pilots by radio, telling them which height to fly at, which way to turn and when to climb or descend.

The basic rule is simple. Two planes must never be closer than a set distance, either up and down or side to side. At cruising height, that is usually 1,000 feet (about 300 m) vertically or several kilometres horizontally. Controllers hand each flight from one team to the next, like a baton in a relay race, from the gate at one airport to the gate at another.

st.prompt: Two airliners are cruising one above the other along the same route. What is the usual smallest gap allowed between them?

options.t: About 300 m
About 30 m
About 3 km

st.reveal: The standard gap at cruising height is 1,000 feet, about 300 m, on most busy routes. Side by side, planes are usually kept several kilometres apart. Together these gaps make a bubble of safe air around each plane.

d.try: Play a controller game with friends. Mark "runways" on the floor with tape and give each "plane" a card with a number. Only the controller can say who moves, using short clear instructions like "Flight 7, turn left, stop". Try it with talking allowed and without, and notice how much safer short, fixed phrases make things.
myth: Once a plane is in the air, the pilot can fly wherever they like.

Airliners follow planned routes called airways, at heights given to them by controllers. A pilot who wants to climb, descend or turn off the route must ask permission first, except in a real emergency.

Flights handled by the US system

sec.t:
In 1929, at Lambert Field in St. Louis, a young pilot named Archie League stood on the airfield with a red flag and a chequered one. Red meant "hold", chequered meant "go". He is often called the first air traffic controller.

Flags worked when only a few planes came in each hour. Soon, controllers used [[@radio-waves|radio]] to talk to pilots instead. After the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], radar arrived: a spinning antenna sends out pulses of radio waves, and echoes bouncing off planes show up as moving dots on a screen.

A tragedy pushed things further. In 1956, two airliners collided over the [[@grand-canyon|Grand Canyon]] in clear weather, outside any radar coverage. Two years later the United States set up a [[federal|federal]] agency to control the country's skies, now called the FAA.

{{story:radio-waves}}

A typical flight passes through several teams. "Ground" controllers guide planes along taxiways. The "tower" clears them for take-off from the runway. "Approach" controllers guide them as they climb away from the airport. Then "centre" controllers, often hundreds of kilometres away, look after them while they cruise.

Each team has its own patch of sky. As a plane reaches the edge, the controller tells the pilot to switch to a new radio frequency and say hello to the next team. In India, the Airports Authority of India runs this system, with large control centres in cities such as Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai.

The job is famously demanding. Controllers train for years, take regular breaks and work in shifts, because a tired mind makes mistakes. Computers help by warning them when two planes are heading for the same patch of sky. Airliners also carry their own collision warning systems, which talk to each other and tell pilots to climb or descend if they ever get too close.

Pilots and controllers use short, fixed phrases so nothing is misunderstood. English is the international language of flying, and letters are spelled with a special alphabet: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta. "Nine" is said "niner", so it is not confused with the German word "nein".

Every plane carries a transponder, a box that answers radar with a four-digit code. Controllers see that code next to the dot on their screens. Some codes have special meanings: 7700 means an emergency, and every controller who sees it pays attention at once.

Radar can only see as far as the horizon, so over the middle of an ocean there is no radar at all. For decades, pilots there reported their position by radio every so often, and planes were kept much farther apart.

Today most airliners broadcast their own position, worked out by [[@gps-how|satellite navigation]], several times a second. [[@satellites-help|Satellites]] and ground stations pick up these signals, so controllers can now track planes in places radar never reached. That has allowed more flights to use the busiest ocean routes safely.

text: [[@how-paper-airplane-best|A paper plane flies far]] when its four forces work well together. Your throw gives it thrust. Its wings make [[lift|lift]] by pushing air down as they move forward. [[drag|Drag]], the push of the air against it, slows it down. And weight pulls it towards the ground.

After it leaves your hand, a paper plane has no engine. From then on it is a [[@gliders|glider]], slowly trading height for distance. The best planes are balanced so they fly level, folded neatly so both sides match, and thrown at the right speed and angle. Good folding matters more than strong arms.

st.prompt: Your paper plane keeps swooping up, stalling and dropping. What should you try?

options.t: Add a paper clip to the nose
Throw it much harder
Bend the back edges of the wings upwards

st.reveal: A plane that swoops up and stalls is usually tail-heavy, or its wing edges are bent up too much. A paper clip on the nose moves the balance point forward, so the plane glides more smoothly.

d.try: Fold one classic dart. Throw it five times and measure each flight in footsteps. Then add a paper clip to the nose and throw it five more times. Next, bend the back edges of the wings up very slightly. Write down which change helped, and remember to change only one thing at a time.
myth: The harder you throw a paper plane, the farther it goes.

Many paper planes loop or dive if thrown too hard. Gliders fly best from a smooth, gentle launch. Only planes built for distance, with stiff, narrow wings, are designed for a hard throw, angled upwards.
facts: weight near the nose, wings bent evenly

sec.t:
Most paper planes fall into two families. Darts are narrow and pointy. They slice through the air with little drag and go fast, so a strong throw sends them a long way, but they don't stay up long.

Gliders have wide wings. They make more lift and fall slowly, so they float gently and stay in the air for a long time. They need a soft, smooth launch. Thrown hard, a glider just loops or crashes.

Real aircraft show the same trade-off. Fighter jets have short, swept-back wings for speed. Gliders and long-distance planes have long, thin wings for lift.

A plane with one wing bigger or more bent than the other will veer off to the side. So the most important rule is [[@symmetry|symmetry]]: both halves should match as closely as possible. Sharp creases help too. Run a fingernail along each fold to make it crisp.

Paper matters a little. Ordinary printer paper works well. Thicker paper keeps its shape but is heavier. Very thin paper is light but floppy. Paper itself was invented in China around 2,000 years ago, and folding it into shapes became the art of origami in Japan. You can read how folding ideas are now used to pack giant [[@telescopes-how|telescopes]] into rockets in [[@origami-maths|how origami is used in space]].

For years, the distance record belonged to an American plane designed by John Collins. In 2012, it was thrown by a former [[@american-football|American football]] player, Joe Ayoob, and flew 69.14 m. In 2022, a team from [[@seoul|South Korea]] beat that record with a flight of more than 77 m. Later that year, an American, Dillon Ruble, reached about 88 m. Then in December 2025, a team of teenagers from China pushed the record to 98.43 m, almost as long as five cricket pitches.

Staying up longest is a different challenge. In 2010, the Japanese engineer Takuo Toda flew a paper plane for 29.2 seconds, launching it straight up so it could glide down in slow circles. His record lasted more than 15 years. In February 2026, a team of teenagers in China kept a paper plane in the air for 31.2 seconds.

Before they built their aeroplane, the [[@wright-brothers|Wright brothers]] tested many small wing shapes in a homemade wind tunnel to see which made the most lift. Engineers today still make simple models before they build the real thing. A sheet of paper, a few folds and a careful throw are a quick way to try out ideas in [[@airplanes-fly|flight]].

text: Peahens choose their mates. In the breeding season, a male raises his long train into a shimmering fan and shakes it, and females look closely before choosing. Over many generations, males with the most impressive displays had more chicks. So the [[gene|genes]] for big, bright trains spread.

Charles Darwin called this sexual selection. It explains why some animals carry features that seem to make life harder, such as giant tails or [[antler|antlers]]. The tail is a cost, but if it wins a mate, it is worth paying. When a peacock shakes its fan, it also makes a low rumble too deep for us to hear, and other peafowl seem to respond to it.

st.prompt: What do you think the tail is for?

options.t: To scare away tigers
To impress peahens
To keep warm

st.reveal: To impress peahens! Females choose which male to pair with, and over many generations they favoured bigger, brighter displays. Charles Darwin called this ‘sexual selection’.
st.nudge: A sudden flash of eyes might startle someone! But the main audience is peahens.

src: Petrie M. et al. (1991) Peahens prefer peacocks with elaborate trains. Animal Behaviour 41.
Freeman A.R. & Hare J.F. (2015) Infrasound in mating displays: a peacock's tale. Animal Behaviour 102.
n.certNote: Female choice is well supported. But studies disagree on which features peahens care about most, and one long study in Japan found no clear preference for showier trains.

d.try: Look at a peacock feather, or a soap bubble, or the shiny side of an old CD. Tilt it slowly under a lamp and watch the colours change. No paint is moving. Light bouncing off tiny layers creates the colours, the same trick a peacock's feathers use.
myth: Peahens lay eggs after drinking the tears of a peacock.
This is an old folk belief, but it isn't true. Peafowl mate like other birds, and the peahen then lays her eggs, usually three to six of them, in a scrape on the ground.

sec.t:
The famous fan is not made of tail feathers. It is a train of about 200 long feathers that grow from the bird's lower back, just above the real tail. The short, stiff tail feathers underneath prop the train up when it is raised.

A peacock grows a new train each year and sheds it after the breeding season. Even with a train up to about 1.5 m long, peacocks can fly. They make short, noisy flights up into trees to roost safely at night.

In 1860, Darwin wrote to a friend that the sight of a peacock's tail feather made him feel sick. His theory of [[evolution|evolution]] explained features that help animals survive. A tail like this seemed to do the opposite. A few years later he worked out that choosing mates could shape animals too.

Scientists still argue about the details. In 1991, a study in England found that peahens preferred males with more eyespots on their trains. But a seven-year study of peafowl in Japan, published in 2008, found no clear preference at all. Peahens may judge several things at once, including the sound and the shaking. Some dinosaurs may have shown off too, as explored in [[@dino-colors|dinosaur colours]].

A displaying peacock does more than stand still. He turns his back, then swings round to face the female. He shakes his raised train so fast that the feathers rattle with a soft, shimmering sound. In 2016, scientists filmed this with [[@how-cameras-speed|high-speed cameras]]. They found that the eyespots stay almost still while the rest of each feather vibrates around them.

Peacocks also have [[@extreme-loudest-animals|one of the loudest calls]] in India, a high "may-awe" that carries far. They call often in the breeding season, which in much of India comes with [[@monsoon|the monsoon]]. In Indian poems and songs, peacocks dance when dark rain clouds gather, an image that has inspired painters and poets for centuries.

The Indian peafowl was named India's national bird in 1963, and it is fully protected by law. Peacocks appear across Indian art and belief. The god Kartikeya, also called Murugan, rides a peacock, and [[@myths-krishna-childhood|Krishna]] is often shown with a peacock feather in his crown. Shah Jahan's jewelled [[@mughals|Peacock Throne]] was named after it.

text: Skydivers fall safely because of air, careful training and backup equipment. When you jump from a plane, [[gravity|gravity]] pulls you faster and faster, but the air pushes back harder as your speed grows. After about 10 to 12 seconds, the two forces balance and you stop speeding up. This top speed is called terminal [[velocity|velocity]], about 200 km/h for someone falling flat.

At a set height, usually around 1,000 to 1,500 m, the skydiver opens a parachute. Its big fabric wing catches the air and slows the fall to about the speed of a gentle jog. The skydiver steers to a landing field and touches down on their feet. Every jumper carries a spare parachute and a small computer that can open it automatically.

st.prompt: A skydiver falling flat on their belly suddenly turns head-down like a diving bird. What happens?

options.t: They fall much faster, up to around 300 km/h
They slow down and float
Nothing changes, because gravity stays the same

st.reveal: Gravity stays the same, but air resistance changes. Head-down, the body cuts through the air like a spear, so it can reach around 300 km/h before the air pushes back hard enough to stop the speeding up.

Fédération Aéronautique Internationale (FAI), world records in parachuting.
Britannica, Skydiving.

d.try: Test air resistance. Drop a flat sheet of paper and a scrunched-up ball of the same paper from the same height at the same time. Watch which lands first. Then fold the sheet into a little cone and try again. Skydivers change their body shape in the same way to fall faster or slower.
myth: In free fall you can't breathe, because the air rushes past too fast.

Skydivers breathe normally. It can feel windy and loud, but there is plenty of air. Only very high jumps, above about 4,500 m, need extra oxygen, and record jumps from the edge of space need a pressure suit.

sec.t:
[[@gravity-fall|Gravity]] tries to make everything fall faster every second. Without air, a skydiver would keep speeding up all the way to the ground.

But air pushes on anything moving through it, a kind of [[@friction|friction]] called drag, like the wind on your hand out of a car window. The faster you go, the harder it pushes. Lying flat on their belly, arms and legs spread, a skydiver acts like a sail. The air soon pushes up as hard as gravity pulls down.

By changing shape, skydivers can change their speed. Arms in and head down, they fall faster. Spread out wide, they fall slower. They also learn to turn, move forward and even link hands with others in the sky.

A skydiver's container holds two parachutes. The main one is folded carefully by the jumper or a trained packer. The reserve parachute must be packed and checked by a certified rigger at regular intervals.

Most jumpers also carry an automatic activation device, or AAD. It is a tiny computer that measures height and speed. If a skydiver is still falling fast near the ground, perhaps because they passed out, it cuts a loop and opens the reserve. AADs have saved many lives.

Skydivers wear an altimeter on the wrist or a beeper in the helmet, warning them when it is time to open.

{{story:parachutes}}

Modern sport parachutes are not round. They are rectangular wings, like a paraglider's, made of cells that fill with air. When the [[canopy|canopy]] opens, the skydiver goes from about 200 km/h to around 15 to 20 km/h in a few seconds.

They pull on steering lines to turn left or right. Just before landing, they pull both lines down together. This "flare" slows them almost to a stop, so they can step onto the ground.

Beginners start with tandem jumps. A student is clipped to the front of an experienced instructor, who handles everything. Students who want to jump alone take courses and practise on the ground for hours first.

Indoor skydiving is another way to learn. A vertical wind tunnel blows air upward at about 200 km/h, so people can float in free fall without ever leaving the ground.

Accidents do happen, but trained skydivers using modern gear have a strong safety record. In the USA, skydivers make millions of jumps each year, and the number of deaths is very small compared with that.

sec.h: Jumps from the edge of space
sec.t:
In 2012, the Austrian Felix Baumgartner rose under a giant helium balloon, a cousin of the [[@hot-air-balloons|hot-air balloon]], to about 39 km, then stepped off. The air up there is so thin that he quickly broke the speed of sound, reaching about 1,358 km/h. He wore a pressure suit, like an astronaut's.

In 2014, the American engineer Alan Eustace went even higher, about 41 km, and set a new record. When anything travels faster than sound, it can make a loud bang, and the science behind it is the [[@sky-sonic-boom|sonic boom]].

text: A kelp forest is an underwater forest made of [[@seaweed-food|giant seaweed]]. Kelp grows in cool, shallow coastal water, anchored to rocks on the sea floor. It reaches up towards the light, sometimes more than 40 m, and spreads out at the surface like a leafy roof. Beneath it, sunlight filters down in green beams, a bit like a forest on land.

Kelp is not really a plant. It is a large brown seaweed, a kind of [[algae|algae]]. But like trees, it gives food and shelter to a huge number of living things: fish, crabs, snails, [[@starfish|sea stars]], sea urchins, seals and sea otters. Kelp forests grow along about a quarter of the world's coastlines, from California and Chile to South Africa, Australia and Norway.

st.prompt: Giant kelp can be over 40 m long, but it has no stiff trunk. How does it stand up in the water?

options.t: Gas-filled bulbs on its blades float it towards the surface

st.reveal: Small balloons of gas grow at the base of many kelp blades. They lift the seaweed towards the sunlit surface, where it spreads out in a floating canopy. A root-like holdfast anchors the bottom to the rocks.

myth: Kelp is a plant.
Kelp looks like a plant and makes food from sunlight, but it is a kind of algae. It has no true roots, flowers or seeds, and it soaks up nutrients through its whole surface.

up to about half a metre a day

sec.t:
Kelp has three main parts. At the bottom is the holdfast, a tangle of root-like grips that clings to rock. It does not suck up water or food like a real root. It just holds on. Above it rises a long, bendy stalk called the stipe. Leafy blades grow from the stipe, and many have small gas-filled bulbs that float them upward.

Kelp makes its own food from sunlight, using [[@photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], just like plants do. It soaks up [[nutrient|nutrients]] from the water through its whole surface. That is why kelp needs cold water: cold water rising from the deep is usually rich in nutrients. Warm, clear [[tropical|tropical]] seas have too few for kelp to grow well.

The health of a kelp forest depends on a balance between hungry animals. Sea urchins, spiny balls that crawl along the bottom, love to chew through kelp holdfasts. When there are too many urchins, they can wipe out a forest and leave bare rock known as an urchin barren.

Sea otters and sunflower sea stars eat urchins and keep their numbers down. When otters were hunted almost to extinction for their fur, many kelp forests collapsed. Where otters have returned, kelp often comes back too, as you can read in [[@sea-otters|sea otters]]. Since 2014, a sea star disease and a long [[@heatwaves|ocean heatwave]] hit northern California hard. Bull kelp forests there shrank by more than 90 per cent, and urchins took over.

People use kelp and other seaweeds in many ways. In Japan and Korea, seaweeds have been eaten for centuries. A substance taken from kelp, called alginate, helps thicken foods. It can help keep [[@ice-cream|ice cream]] smooth, and it turns up in some [[@made-toothpaste|toothpastes]] and medicines.

India has no giant kelp forests, because its seas are too warm. But seaweeds of other kinds grow along its coasts. In Tamil Nadu, around the Gulf of Mannar, many families farm and collect seaweed, which is sold to make thickeners for foods and other products. Seaweed farming is growing in India, and scientists are studying how to do it without harming the [[@coral-reefs|reefs]] nearby.

text: Most ocean waves are made by wind. When wind blows across calm water, it rubs the surface and makes small ripples. The ripples give the wind something to push against, so they grow into bigger and bigger waves. The [[@wind-blows|wind]] passes its energy to the water.

Three things decide how big waves get: how strong the wind is, how long it blows, and how much open water it blows across. Sailors call that stretch of open water the fetch. A light breeze over a pond makes ripples. A powerful storm blowing for days over thousands of kilometres of open ocean can raise waves taller than a house. Once made, waves can travel huge distances, long after the storm that made them has died away.

st.reveal: Out in deep water, a wave carries energy, not water. The duck rises and falls in a little loop as each wave passes. Only near the shore, where waves break, does water rush forward and carry things with it.

myth: Every seventh wave is the biggest.

Waves often arrive in groups called sets, with some bigger than others, but there is no fixed pattern. The biggest wave in a set can come at any point, which is why surfers and swimmers keep watching.

sec.t:
A wave is a moving bump of energy, not a moving river of water. As a wave passes, each bit of water near the surface moves in a circle: up, forward, down and back. Then it is roughly where it began. That is why [[@ocean-currents-travel|a floating bottle]] out at sea mostly bobs in place.

Waves on a skipping rope work the same way. If you shake one end, a wave travels to the other end, but the rope itself doesn't go anywhere. Sound is a wave too, travelling through air instead of water, as you can read in [[@sound-travel|how sound travels]].

The circles get smaller with depth. A few tens of metres down, even a large storm wave is hardly felt. [[@submarines|Submarines]] dive below rough weather for this reason.

Near the shore, things change. As a wave moves into shallow water, its bottom starts to drag on the sea floor and slows down. The top keeps going faster. The wave grows taller and steeper, until the top tips over and crashes forward. That is a breaking wave.

The shape of the beach decides how waves break. On a gently sloping beach, waves spill over slowly in a line of white foam. On a steep beach or a sudden reef, they curl over into a hollow tube before they crash, the kind surfers love. [[@sport-surfing|Surfing]] itself grew up in Hawaii, where people rode waves on wooden boards long before European sailors arrived, as you can read in [[@hawaii-culture|Hawaiian culture]].

sec.h: Not all waves come from wind
sec.t:
A [[@tsunami|tsunami]] is a different kind of wave. Its name is Japanese for "harbour wave", one of many [[@words-borrowed|words English has borrowed]]. It is usually caused by an [[@earthquakes|earthquake]] under the sea, which suddenly lifts or drops a huge amount of water. Out in the open ocean, [[@tsunami-warning|a tsunami]] may be less than a metre high and pass under ships unnoticed, but it moves as fast as a jet plane. When it reaches shallow water, it rears up into a wall of water. The 2004 Indian Ocean [[tsunami|tsunami]] struck the coasts of India, Sri Lanka, [[@thailand|Thailand]] and Indonesia.

Tides are waves too, of a sort: the longest waves on Earth, pulled along by the Moon and Sun, as explained in [[@tides|tides]]. On India's west coast, the [[monsoon|monsoon]] brings rough seas from June, and fishing boats stay home for safety. The people who fish there learn to read waves from childhood, as you can see in [[@fishing-boats|how India's fishing communities read the sea]].

text: Trees don't have a heart to pump water. Instead, water evaporates from tiny holes in the leaves, and that pulls the next bit of water up behind it, all the way from the roots, like a very long, thin straw. Redwoods are champions at this.

The tallest known tree, a coast redwood named Hyperion, is about 116 m tall, taller than a 30-storey building. That's about one and a half times the height of the Qutub Minar in Delhi, and taller than the [[@statue-liberty|Statue of Liberty]] from the ground to the tip of her torch.

st.prompt: How does water get to the top of a redwood?

options.t: The tree pumps it with a heart
Water evaporating from leaves pulls more water up
Rain fills the trunk from the top

st.reveal: As water evaporates from the leaves, it pulls on the water below it, like sucking through a very long, thin straw. Redwoods also soak up fog through their leaves.

The next day, ask an adult to cut the stalk across and look for coloured dots. Those are the tubes that carry water up, the same kind that lift water 100 metres in a redwood.
myth: The tallest trees must have the deepest roots to hold them up.

Redwood roots are surprisingly shallow, usually only a few metres deep. They spread out wide instead, often 30 metres or more, and tangle with the roots of neighbouring trees, so a grove holds itself up together.

sec.t:
Water moves up a tree through bundles of microscopic tubes in the wood. Water [[molecule|molecules]] cling tightly to each other, so a column of water behaves a bit like a chain. When one molecule evaporates from a leaf, it tugs on the one below, and that tugs on the next, all the way down to the roots.

There is a limit. The higher the water climbs, the harder [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] pulls against it, and the more slowly it reaches the top. In 2004, a team led by George Koch climbed some of the tallest redwoods to study their highest leaves. Those leaves were small and thirsty. The scientists calculated that redwoods probably can't grow much taller than about 122 to 130 metres.

In 2006, two naturalists, Chris Atkins and Michael Taylor, were hiking through a remote valley in Redwood [[@national-parks|National Park]] when they spotted an unusually tall tree. A scientist later climbed it and dropped a tape measure from the top. It measured about 116 metres, making it the tallest known living tree.

The park has kept its location secret to protect it. When too many visitors went looking for it anyway, trampling the ground around its roots, the park closed the area. Today visitors who go there can be fined.

Redwood bark can be 30 cm thick and contains chemicals that resist fire and insects. Some redwoods are [[@trees-oldest|more than 2,000 years old]].

[[@forest-fires|Forest fires]] that kill other trees often leave redwoods scarred but alive. When a redwood is cut down or knocked over, new shoots sprout from its stump and roots. Over many years they grow into a circle of trees around the old one, which people call a "fairy ring".

In the 1800s and early 1900s, loggers cut most of the old redwood forests for timber. Today only a small fraction of the original old-growth forest is left, mostly in protected parks. Groups such as the Save the Redwoods League, founded in 1918, bought land to protect, and Redwood National Park was set up in 1968.

Redwoods have cousins. The giant sequoia, which grows inland in the Sierra Nevada, is shorter but much thicker, the biggest tree on Earth by volume. A third relative, the dawn redwood, was known only from [[fossil|fossils]] until living trees were found in China in the 1940s.

The tallest tree is in California. The tree that spreads over the most ground is in India: the [[@banyan|Great Banyan]] near Kolkata, or Thimmamma Marrimanu in Andhra Pradesh, which holds the world record. One reaches up, the other reaches out.

text: Kangaroos hop so far because their back legs work like giant pogo sticks. Long, stretchy [[tendon|tendons]] run down the back of each leg. When a kangaroo lands, those tendons stretch and store energy, like a spring being squashed. On the next jump the energy is released and flings the animal forward again.

A big red kangaroo can cover about 8 m in one bound and race at over 50 km/h for short bursts. Its thick tail acts as a balance beam behind it. And once it gets going, hopping faster costs it hardly any extra energy, which no running human can claim.

st.prompt: When a kangaroo speeds up from a gentle hop to a fast bound, what happens to the energy it uses?

options.t: It doubles
It stays roughly the same
It drops to almost nothing

st.reveal: Over a wide range of speeds, a hopping kangaroo uses about the same energy. Its leg tendons work like springs, storing energy as it lands and giving it back on the next jump. Running humans burn more energy the faster they go.

src: Dawson T. J. and Taylor C. R. (1973), energetic cost of locomotion in kangaroos, Nature.

d.try: Mark a starting line, then see how far you can jump with feet together from standing. Measure it with a tape or by counting your shoe lengths. A big red kangaroo's 8 m bound is probably around five times your best jump.
myth: The word kangaroo comes from an Aboriginal phrase meaning "I don't understand you".
That story is false. Captain James Cook's crew recorded the word in 1770 from the Guugu Yimithirr people of north Queensland, whose word gangurru names a large grey kangaroo.

sec.t:
The secret is in the tendons, the tough cords joining muscle to bone. A kangaroo's leg tendons are long and elastic. At each landing the animal's weight stretches them. Then they snap back, much as a stretched rubber band does.

That means the muscles don't have to start every jump from scratch. A large share of each hop is powered by energy recycled from the hop before. It is the same principle as the metal [[@springs|springs]] in a trampoline or a mattress.

Hopping is great for speed but clumsy for shuffling around while grazing. So at slow speeds, kangaroos do something strange. They put their front paws and tail on the ground, then swing both back legs forward together.

A 2014 study found the tail pushes as hard as the front and back legs put together during this slow walk. Scientists now describe the tail as working like a fifth leg. Kangaroos also find it very hard to walk backwards, partly because of that big tail and their long feet. Put a kangaroo in water, though, and it changes style completely. It swims well, kicking its back legs one at a time.

Kangaroos are [[marsupial|marsupials]], [[mammal|mammals]] whose babies finish growing in a pouch. A red kangaroo joey is born after only about 33 days. It is about 2 cm long and weighs less than a gram, smaller than a jellybean.

The tiny, blind newborn crawls through its mother's fur to the pouch, using its front legs. Inside, it latches on to a teat and stays for many months. Mothers can even pause the growth of a second, tiny embryo until the pouch is free again. Australia has plenty of other odd mammals, from the egg-laying [[@power-platypus|platypus]] to the [[@wild-koala|koala]].

Kangaroos are common across much of [[@australia|Australia]]. In 2022 surveys, about 36 million were counted in the areas where governments track them. Australia's human population is about 27 million. Numbers rise after rainy years and crash in [[drought|droughts]], sometimes by half.

Big males stand about as tall as a grown man, and they fight by leaning back on their tails and kicking with both feet. Still, the hop is the real superpower. A champion human high jumper clears about 2.4 m, and the science of [[@sport-science-high-jump|jumping humans]] shows how hard we work for every centimetre that a kangaroo gets for free.

text: A fridge door is wrapped in a thin skin of steel, and steel is mostly iron. Iron is one of the few materials a magnet can really pull on. When you press a magnet against the door, it tugs on the iron, and that tug is strong enough to hold up the magnet and a sheet of paper or two.

The flat, bendy magnets that come free with pizza menus are cleverer than they look. They are made of a powder called ferrite, a kind of iron oxide (close cousin of rust), mixed into rubber. A factory then magnetises them in thin stripes, north, south, north, south. That pattern pushes most of the pull out of the back, so the front hardly sticks at all.

st.prompt: You flip a flat rubber fridge magnet over and press its printed side against the fridge. What happens?

options.t: It barely sticks, because the strong side is the back
It sticks just as well on both sides
It pushes away from the fridge

st.reveal: Flexible magnets are made with stripes of north and south poles that send most of their pull out of one face. The printed face gets only a weak leftover field, so the magnet slides off.

myth: Magnets stick to all metals.

sec.h: Tiny compass needles inside the iron
sec.t:
Inside a piece of iron are billions of microscopic regions called domains. Each one behaves like a tiny compass needle. Normally they point every which way and cancel out, so a nail isn't magnetic. Bring a magnet close and many of those needles swing round to line up with it. For a moment the steel door becomes a weak magnet itself, pointing the opposite way, and opposites attract.

That is why the pull vanishes when you take the magnet away. The domains relax and go back to pointing anywhere. A [[@steel|steel]] spoon behaves the same way, and so does a paper clip. Aluminium cans, copper wires and gold rings don't have domains that line up like this, so magnets ignore them.

sec.h: How strong is a fridge magnet?

sec.t:
Every fridge already has a long magnet built in. Look at the soft rubber strip around the door. Hidden inside is a flexible magnetic strip that pulls the door tight against the steel frame and keeps cold air in.

There is a serious story behind it. Old fridges in the USA shut with metal latches that could only be opened from outside. Children playing hide-and-seek sometimes climbed into old fridges dumped in yards and got trapped. In 1956, the US Refrigerator Safety Act required doors that could be pushed open from the inside. Magnetic seals solved it neatly. A child can push the door open, yet it still closes tightly enough to keep milk cold.

sec.h: Why some fridges won't hold a magnet
sec.t:
If you have tried to stick a holiday souvenir to a shiny new fridge and it slid straight down, you weren't imagining it. Many modern fridges use stainless steel. Some types of stainless steel contain a lot of nickel and chromium, arranged in a way that stops the domains forming. They look like steel but are almost invisible to a magnet.

Manufacturers sometimes add a magnetic layer to stainless doors because so many families complained. In India and the USA alike, the fridge door has quietly become the family noticeboard. Timetables, menus, drawings and wedding cards all hang there, held up by iron powder and rubber.

And the strangest part? A [[@magnets-how|compass needle]] is just a skinny magnet like the one on your [[@refrigerator|refrigerator]]. It swings north because it is feeling a far bigger magnet, made by swirling molten iron thousands of kilometres under your feet: [[@earth-magnet|Earth itself]].

text: A farmer's year is shaped by seasons. In India there are two big ones. The kharif season begins with the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] in June or July, when rice, cotton and soybeans go into wet fields. The rabi season begins after the rains, around October, when wheat, mustard and chickpeas are sown for a spring harvest.

Between those two, there is ploughing, weeding, watering, spraying, harvesting and selling. Farmers also look after animals, mend tools and worry about prices. Some fit in a third, short summer crop called zaid, such as watermelons and cucumbers.

st.reveal: Wheat is a rabi crop. It is sown in the cool months after the rains, grows through winter on stored soil water and irrigation, and is harvested around March and April.

sec.h: October to March: the winter crop
sec.t:
After the rice is cut, threshed and sold, the same field may be ready for wheat. In Punjab and Haryana, farmers sow wheat in November and watch it turn from green to gold by April. The cool nights help the grain fill out. A sudden hot spell in March can shrink the harvest.

This is also when a farmer's mind turns to money. Seeds, [[fertiliser|fertiliser]], diesel and labour are paid for months before any crop is sold. Many farmers borrow, and a bad season can leave them in debt. That is why the government buys some crops at a fixed minimum price, and why prices are argued about so fiercely.

Across India, the end of a harvest is a reason to celebrate. Baisakhi in Punjab marks the wheat harvest. Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Bihu in Assam and [[@onam-pongal|Onam]] in Kerala all have roots in the farming calendar. Cooking new rice with jaggery and milk at Pongal is, quite literally, tasting the year's work.

In the USA, Thanksgiving grew out of autumn harvest feasts too.

In the American Midwest, the [[rhythm|rhythm]] is different. A corn farmer in Iowa plants in April and May, once the frozen ground has thawed. The fields grow all summer and are harvested between September and November by combine harvesters whose cutting bars are nearly as wide as a school bus is long. Winter is for fixing machines, planning and selling grain.

American farms are huge. In 2022 the average farm covered about 187 hectares. In India, the average is about one hectare, roughly the size of a football field and a half. So one American farmer with machines might work land that, in India, would be split into about 170 family farms.

In 2025, a little over 40% of India's workers still earned their living mainly from farming, though that share has been falling for decades. In the USA, fewer than 2 in every 100 workers farm. Yet both countries grow far more food than they did 60 years ago, thanks partly to the [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]], better seeds and [[irrigation|irrigation]].

Farmers have also learned to work together. Dairy [[@cooperatives|cooperatives]] in Gujarat turned millions of small herds into one of the world's biggest milk businesses. The wheat in a roti on a Delhi dinner table was probably sown in November by someone who spent the winter watching the sky.

text: Armed forces are a country's military: its army on land, navy at sea and air force in the sky. Their main job is to defend the country from attack and protect its borders, coasts and airspace.

But that is only part of what they do. They rescue people from floods and earthquakes, carry supplies to cut-off areas, evacuate citizens from war zones abroad and serve as United Nations peacekeepers. In most [[democracy|democracies]], including India and the USA, the armed forces take orders from the elected government, not the other way round. This is called civilian control.

Whichever general has served longest

st.reveal: The President of India is the Supreme Commander, but acts on the advice of the elected government, led by the Prime Minister and the Defence Minister. This principle, called civilian control, keeps the military answerable to the people.

sec.t:
India's Army is one of the largest in the world. It guards long land borders, from the deserts of Rajasthan to the icy heights of Ladakh and the forests of the north-east. The Navy patrols the Indian Ocean, and the Air Force flies fighter jets, transport planes and [[@helicopters|helicopters]]. A separate Coast Guard watches India's coastline.

In 2019, the government created the post of Chief of Defence Staff, to help the three services plan and work together. Army Day, on 15 January, marks the day in 1949 when K. M. Cariappa became the first Indian commander-in-chief of the Indian Army.

The forces have changed in other ways too. In 2016, the Air Force commissioned its first three women [[@jobs-pilot|fighter pilots]], and women now serve in many roles once closed to them. Soldiers, sailors and air crew join from every state. Many army regiments still carry old names of regions and communities, such as the Madras Regiment, the Sikh Regiment and the Gorkha Rifles.

{{story:world-war-two}}

When floods struck [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]] in June 2013, roads were washed away and thousands of pilgrims and villagers were stranded. The Army built temporary bridges and the Air Force flew helicopter missions to lift people out. In 2018, during the [[@floods-why|Kerala floods]], military helicopters plucked people off rooftops, and Navy boats reached flooded villages.

The forces also help abroad. After a huge earthquake in Turkey and Syria in 2023, India sent [[@people-army-life|army doctors]] and rescue teams. The US military often carries aid to disaster zones around the world, using its large fleet of ships and transport planes.

The USA has six military services: the Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Coast Guard and Space Force. The Space Force, set up in December 2019, looks after military satellites. The US military has bases in many countries and spends more than any other in the world.

The US President is commander in chief, but only Congress can formally declare war. This split was deliberate. The writers of the Constitution did not want one person to be able to take the country into war alone.

In 1948, after a short civil war, Costa Rica in Central America abolished its army. Its leader, José Figueres, wanted the money spent on education and health instead. Today the country has police but no military, and it is known for its schools, health care and protected forests.

Most countries still keep armed forces, and [[@world-war-two|world wars]] in the last century showed what happens when they are used on a huge scale. That is one reason the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] was created, to settle disputes before they turn into fighting. Some people argue that strong armies prevent wars by making attack too risky, while others think spending on weapons makes conflict more likely. Countries have argued about that balance for centuries.

text: India's tribal communities, often called Adivasis, meaning "original inhabitants", are groups with their own languages, customs, beliefs and histories. The government lists over 700 of them as Scheduled Tribes, giving them special protections and benefits in the [[@constitution|Constitution]].

The 2011 Census counted about 10.4 crore people in Scheduled Tribes, around 8.6 percent of India's population. They live in almost every state, with large numbers in central India, the northeast and hilly or forested regions. The Bhils of western India and the Gonds of central India are the largest groups, each with well over a crore people.

st.prompt: Which Indian state or union territory has the highest share of tribal people?

Uttar Pradesh

st.reveal: In the 2011 Census, about 95 percent of Lakshadweep's people and about 94 percent of Mizoram's were listed as Scheduled Tribes. Some places, such as Punjab, Haryana and Delhi, have no Scheduled Tribes at all on the official list.

myth: India's tribal people all live in forests and follow the same way of life.

Tribal communities are hugely varied. Some are farmers, herders or fishers, many live in towns and cities, and members work as teachers, doctors, athletes and politicians. India's President Droupadi Murmu, elected in 2022, is from the Santhal community.

sec.t:
Some of India's best-known art comes from tribal communities. [[@warli|Warli]] painters in Maharashtra use circles, triangles and lines to show dancing villagers and harvests. Gond artists in Madhya Pradesh fill animals and trees with patterns of dots and dashes. Saura paintings from Odisha, Bhil art and the metal-casting craft of dhokra are prized around the world.

The Gond artist Jangarh Singh Shyam helped bring [[@gond-art|Gond art]] to galleries in the 1980s. Today, the work of many tribal artists sells in cities from Delhi to New York, and hangs in museums in both.

Tribal people speak hundreds of languages from several language families. Some, like Santali, Gondi, Bhili and Mundari, have millions of speakers. Others are spoken by only a few hundred people and are in danger of disappearing.

In 1925, Raghunath Murmu, a Santhal teacher, created the Ol Chiki script for Santali. In 2003, Santali was added to the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution as one of India's official scheduled languages. Smaller languages face a harder road, explored in [[@people-languages-dying|dying languages]].

Tribal communities have a long history of standing up for their land. Birsa Munda led the Munda people against British rule and unfair landlords in the 1890s, and died in prison aged about 25. Since 2021, his birthday, 15 November, has been marked as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas, Tribal Pride Day.

Many tribal families have faced loss of land to dams, mines and forest laws, and many still have less access to schools and hospitals. Laws such as the Forest Rights Act of 2006 aim to protect their rights to land and forest produce.

Seventy-five communities are listed as Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups, because they are small in number or live very isolated lives. They include the Jarawa and Sentinelese of the Andaman Islands. The Sentinelese, on North Sentinel Island, avoid all contact with outsiders. Indian law forbids visiting them, both to respect their choice and to protect them from diseases they have no immunity to.

The USA has its own first peoples, more than 570 federally recognised tribes, from the Navajo to the Cherokee. Like Adivasis in India, they speak many languages, keep old traditions alive and have struggled for land rights. Comparing the two is a good way to understand the story of [[@native-nations|Native nations]].

text: Swami Vivekananda was an Indian monk and teacher who lived from 1863 to 1902. He was a follower of the saint Sri Ramakrishna and helped bring the ideas of Vedanta, a school of Hindu [[philosophy|philosophy]], and of yoga to the West.

He became famous after a speech in [[@chicago|Chicago]] in 1893, at a gathering of religious leaders from around the world. Back in India he founded the Ramakrishna Mission, which still runs schools, hospitals and relief work.
He urged Indians, especially young people, to be strong, confident and of service to the poor. His birthday, 12 January, is National Youth Day in India.

sec.t:
Vivekananda was born Narendranath Datta in Calcutta, now Kolkata, in 1863. Friends called him Naren. He was clever, sporty and loved music, and he asked hard questions.

Bengal was full of new ideas at the time, a period called the [[@bengali-renaissance|Bengal Renaissance]]. Naren read Western philosophy at college. But one question bothered him: had anyone actually seen God?

He put it to many teachers. In 1881 he met Sri Ramakrishna, a priest at the Dakshineswar temple near Calcutta. Ramakrishna is said to have answered simply that yes, he had. Naren was puzzled, then drawn in, and became his student.

After Ramakrishna died in 1886, Naren and other young followers became monks. He later took the name Vivekananda.

For several years he travelled across India, often on foot, carrying little more than a staff and a bowl. He stayed with rajas and with the poor. The hunger and hardship he saw troubled him deeply.

In December 1892 he reached [[@kanyakumari|Kanyakumari]], at India's southern tip. According to tradition he swam out to a rock in the sea and meditated there for three days. There he decided to go to the West, both to share India's ideas and to seek help for its people. The Vivekananda Rock Memorial now stands on that rock.

{{story:speeches-famous}}

In 1893 Chicago hosted a World's Fair, and alongside it a World's Parliament of Religions. Vivekananda arrived with little money and no official invitation, and friends he made in the USA helped him get a place.

On 11 September he stood up to speak. His first words, "Sisters and brothers of America", brought thousands of people to their feet in applause that went on for minutes. His speech was short. He spoke about tolerance, saying that different religions are like rivers with different sources that all reach the same sea.

American newspapers wrote about him. He spent the next few years lecturing in the USA and Britain and set up the Vedanta Society in New York in 1894.

Vivekananda came home in 1897 as a hero. That year he founded the Ramakrishna Mission. Its idea was that serving people, especially the poor and sick, is a way of serving God.

The Mission's headquarters is at Belur Math, on the Hooghly near Kolkata. Today it runs schools, colleges, hospitals and help for people hit by floods, [[cyclone|cyclones]] and other disasters, in India and abroad.

He died at Belur Math on 4 July 1902, aged only 39.

Vivekananda's words gave confidence to many Indians under British rule. Leaders of the [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]], including Subhas Chandra Bose, said his writings inspired them. Since 1985 India has marked his birthday as National Youth Day.

Not everyone agrees with all his views. Some historians point out that he spoke about Hinduism in ways that suited his time and audience, and people still debate how he should be remembered. But his call to young people, "Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached", is still painted on school walls across India.

text: A chart turns a pile of numbers into a picture. Our eyes are much quicker at comparing lengths, heights and slopes than at comparing columns of figures.

Different charts tell different kinds of story. A bar chart compares amounts, like how many runs each batter scored. A line graph shows change over time, like the temperature through a day. A pie chart shows how a whole is split into parts, like how a family spends its money. A map can show where things happen.
The trick is choosing the picture that makes the pattern jump out, and drawing it honestly.

sec.t:
Before the late 1700s, people mostly shared numbers in tables. Then a Scottish engineer named William Playfair had an idea. In 1786 he published a book about England's trade with other countries, and instead of only listing figures, he drew them.

He used lines rising and falling across years to show [[import|imports]] and [[export|exports]]. He drew bars to compare different countries. In 1801 he added the first pie chart. It took decades for his ideas to catch on. Today the charts he drew are in almost every newspaper and textbook.

Florence Nightingale is famous as the "lady with the lamp" who cared for British soldiers during the Crimean War in the 1850s. She was also a gifted mathematician.

She noticed that far more soldiers were dying of diseases like cholera and typhus than of their wounds. Dirty, crowded [[@hospitals|hospitals]] were to blame. To make government officials pay attention, she drew a new kind of chart in 1858. It looked like a flower, with a wedge for each month. Blue wedges showed deaths from disease, and they were enormous next to the rest.

The chart was hard to ignore. It helped persuade the army to improve cleanliness, fresh air and drains in its hospitals. Soon afterwards she became the first woman elected to Britain's Royal Statistical Society.

sec.t:
Some charts become famous because they make a big idea simple. Graphs of global temperatures rising since the 1800s have helped millions of people understand [[@climate-change|climate change]]. Every ten years, a [[@census|census]] produces charts showing how a country's population is growing and moving.

Good chart makers follow a few habits. They label the [[axis|axes]]. They start bar charts at zero. They don't use 3D effects that make some slices look bigger than they are.

Because charts are persuasive, they can also be used to trick people. A bar chart where the axis starts at 95 instead of 0 can make a tiny difference look huge. A line graph squeezed sideways can make a slow change look like a sudden jump.

That is why it is always worth checking the numbers along the edges before believing the shape. You can read more about these tricks in [[@statistics-lies|Can numbers lie?]]

text: To count money quickly, sort it first. Put all the notes and coins of the same value together. Then count the pile with the biggest value first, and work down to the smallest.
Group things into tens or hundreds as you go. Ten ₹10 coins make ₹100. Five ₹20 notes make ₹100 too. Making friendly round totals keeps the numbers small in your head.
And to give change, try counting up from the price to the amount paid, the way many shopkeepers do. It is quicker than subtracting and harder to get wrong.

st.reveal: From 63 to 70 is 7, and from 70 to 100 is 30. So the change is 37. Breaking the gap into friendly steps that end in zero is much easier than subtracting in your head.

sec.t:
When money is mixed up, your brain has to keep switching. Ten, then fifty, then two, then a hundred. It is easy to lose track.

Sorting turns one hard job into several easy ones. A pile of ₹500 notes is counted in five hundreds: 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000. A pile of ₹2 coins is counted in twos. Skip counting like this is simple once you have practised your [[@multiplication-tables|times tables]].

Bank cashiers also face all the notes the same way up and the same way round. That way, a fake or a note of the wrong value stands out at once.

Say a toy costs ₹63 and you hand over ₹100. Many people try to work out 100 minus 63 in their heads, which means borrowing and carrying.

A shopkeeper often does it differently. Starting at 63, they hand you ₹2 and say "65", then ₹5 and say "70". Then come ₹10 and ₹20: "80, 100." The change is ₹37, and you have watched it being counted out.

This counting-up method is a favourite of [[@mental-maths|mental maths]] experts too. You jump to the nearest round number first, then add in big friendly steps.

India's banknotes come in different sizes and colours, and many have raised marks you can feel, such as small bumps, lines or shapes, near the edge. These help people who are blind or have low vision tell notes apart.

In 2020 the Reserve Bank of India launched a free app called MANI, short for Mobile Aided Note Identifier. Point a phone camera at a note, and it says the value out loud.

In the USA all paper dollars are the same size and colour, which makes them harder to tell apart by touch. Many blind Americans fold different notes in different ways, and the government offers free electronic readers.

Money keeps changing. India stopped printing ₹2,000 notes and in 2023 began taking them back from circulation. In 2025 the USA made its last pennies for everyday use, because each one cost more than a cent to make.

Many people now pay by phone. In India, [[@upi-payments|UPI]] payments are so common that even small tea stalls display a QR code. Yet counting money is still a useful skill. It keeps your brain quick with numbers, helps you spot a mistake in your change, and makes it easier to understand bigger numbers like [[@lakh-crore|lakhs and crores]].

text: हड्डियाँ ज़्यादातर अपने सिरों पर बढ़ती हैं। जाँघ की हड्डी जैसी किसी लंबी हड्डी के हर सिरे के पास नरम [[tissue|ऊतक]] की एक चकती होती है, जिसे ग्रोथ प्लेट कहते हैं। यह [[cartilage|उपास्थि]] से बनी होती है, वही लचीली चीज़ जो तुम्हारे कानों और नाक की नोक में है। ग्रोथ प्लेट की कोशिकाएँ बढ़ती रहती हैं, और नई उपास्थि धीरे-धीरे सख़्त हड्डी में बदलती जाती है, जिससे सिरे और दूर खिसकते जाते हैं। इसी से तुम लंबे होते हो।

जब कोई हड्डी टूटती है, तो शरीर उसे कई चरणों में दोबारा बनाता है: पहले खून का थक्का, फिर नए ऊतक का एक नरम पुल, फिर सख़्त हड्डी। बच्चों में टूटी हुई बाँह की सीधी-सादी हड्डी अक्सर तीन से छह हफ़्ते में जुड़ जाती है, बड़ों से कहीं जल्दी।

नवजात शिशु में लगभग 300 हड्डियाँ और हड्डियों की शुरुआतें होती हैं, जिनमें से बहुत-सी अभी कुछ हद तक उपास्थि की बनी होती हैं। बच्चे के बढ़ने के साथ इनमें से कुछ आपस में जुड़ जाती हैं। जैसे खोपड़ी अलग-अलग प्लेटों से शुरू होती है, जिनके बीच नरम जगहें होती हैं। इसी वजह से जन्म के समय बच्चे का सिर दबकर बाहर आ पाता है। ज़िंदगी के पहले कुछ सालों में ये प्लेटें आपस में जुड़ जाती हैं। रीढ़ के निचले सिरे और कूल्हों की हड्डियाँ भी जुड़ जाती हैं।

बड़े होने तक गिनती 206 पर टिक जाती है। इनमें से आधी से ज़्यादा हाथों और पैरों में हैं।

हड्डी टूटने के कुछ ही घंटों में टूटी जगह के आसपास खून इकट्ठा होकर थक्का बना लेता है। अगले कुछ दिनों में कोशिकाएँ वहाँ पहुँचती हैं और उपास्थि व मज़बूत रेशों का एक नरम पुल बनाती हैं, जिसे कैलस कहते हैं। कई हफ़्तों में हड्डी बनाने वाली कोशिकाएँ इस कैलस को सख़्त हड्डी में बदल देती हैं।

इसके बाद महीनों तक शरीर मरम्मत को नया आकार देता रहता है, और फ़ालतू हड्डी हटाता रहता है, जब तक कि वह लगभग नई जैसी न दिखने लगे। डॉक्टर का काम है टूटे सिरों को सीधा मिलाना और उन्हें बिना हिले टिकाए रखना, अक्सर प्लास्टर चढ़ाकर, ताकि हड्डी सीधी जुड़े। [[@x-rays|एक्स-रे]] से पता चलता है कि हड्डी ठीक से जुड़ रही है या नहीं।

बच्चों की हड्डियाँ बड़ों से ज़्यादा लचीली होती हैं, इसलिए कभी-कभी वे एक खास ढंग से टूटती हैं, जिसे ग्रीनस्टिक फ़्रैक्चर कहते हैं। हड्डी मुड़ जाती है और सिर्फ़ एक तरफ़ से चटकती है, जैसे किसी पेड़ की हरी, ताज़ा टहनी, जो साफ़-साफ़ दो टुकड़े नहीं होती।

शरीर का लगभग 99% कैल्शियम हड्डियों और दाँतों में जमा रहता है। कैल्शियम [[@milk|दूध]], दही, पनीर, रागी, हरी पत्तेदार सब्ज़ियों और तिल जैसे खाने से आता है। विटामिन डी, जो धूप में तुम्हारी त्वचा खुद बनाती है, आँतों को यह कैल्शियम सोखने में मदद करता है।

हड्डियाँ इस्तेमाल का जवाब भी देती हैं। दौड़ना, कूदना, रस्सी कूदना और नाचना हड्डियों पर अच्छा दबाव डालते हैं, और हड्डियाँ जवाब में और ठोस हो जाती हैं। लोग अपनी हड्डियों की ज़्यादातर ताकत बचपन और किशोर उम्र में जुटाते हैं, और यह लगभग 28-29 साल की उम्र तक अपने चरम पर पहुँचती है।
