हर बाल की जड़ में, त्वचा के नीचे, एक छोटी-सी थैली होती है जिसे [[follicle|फ़ॉलिकल]] कहते हैं। इसके अंदर मेलानोसाइट नाम की खास कोशिकाएँ मेलानिन बनाती हैं और बढ़ते हुए नए बाल में भर देती हैं। बाल के त्वचा से बाहर निकलते ही वह ज़िंदा नहीं रहता, और उसका रंग पक्का हो जाता है।

[[pigment|वर्णक]] बाल के अंदर ठसे नन्हे दानों के रूप में होता है। काले बाल गहरे दानों से भरे होते हैं। सुनहरे बालों में बस कुछ ही दाने होते हैं, इसलिए रोशनी आर-पार होकर बिखर जाती है और बाल सुनहरे दिखते हैं। लाल बालों में फ़ियोमेलानिन एक गर्म नारंगी चमक देता है।

ऑस्ट्रेलिया के उत्तर-पूर्व में सोलोमन द्वीपों के बहुत-से बच्चों की त्वचा साँवली होती है और बाल चमकीले सुनहरे। बरसों तक लोग अंदाज़ा लगाते रहे कि यह यूरोपीय नाविकों या व्यापारियों की देन होगी। 2012 में वैज्ञानिकों ने द्वीपवासियों के DNA की जाँच की और पाया कि सुनहरे बाल एक दूसरे जीन में बदलाव से आते हैं, जो यूरोपीय लोगों में लगभग कभी नहीं मिलता।

यानी सुनहरे बाल कम से कम दो बार, अलग-अलग जगहों पर और अलग-अलग तरीकों से, [[evolve|विकसित]] हुए। बालों का रंग बहुत-से जीन तय करते हैं, सौ से भी ज़्यादा, इसलिए एक ही रंगत तक पहुँचने के बहुत-से रास्ते हैं।

बहुत-से बच्चे हल्के रंग के बालों के साथ पैदा होते हैं और बढ़ते-बढ़ते उनके बाल गहरे हो जाते हैं, क्योंकि शरीर ज़्यादा यूमेलानिन बनाने लगता है। कुछ बच्चे घने काले बालों के साथ पैदा होते हैं, जो झड़कर हल्के रंग के उगते हैं। गर्मियों की धूप बालों के सिरों को फीका कर सकती है, क्योंकि पराबैंगनी रोशनी धीरे-धीरे मेलानिन को तोड़ देती है। वे फीके सिरे मरे हुए बाल हैं, इसलिए कटने तक हल्के ही रहते हैं।

आगे चलकर मेलानोसाइट धीरे-धीरे काम करना बंद कर देते हैं। नए बाल कम से कम वर्णक के साथ उगते जाते हैं, और आखिर में सफ़ेद हो जाते हैं। सफ़ेद और काले बालों का मेल खिचड़ी दिखता है। ज़्यादातर लोगों के [[@grey-hair|बाल पकने]] 30 या 40 की उम्र के आसपास शुरू होते हैं, और कब, यह ज़्यादातर जीन पर टिका है।

लोग हज़ारों साल से अपने बालों का रंग बदलते आए हैं। भारत में वही पौधा जिससे [[@mehendi|मेहंदी]] लगाई जाती है, लंबे समय से बालों को लाल-भूरा रंगने के काम आता रहा है। आज दुकानों में काले से लेकर चटक नीले तक हर रंग की डाई बिकती है।

तुम्हारे बालों का कुदरती रंग इस बारे में बहुत कम बताता है कि तुम कौन हो, पर उसमें तुम्हारे परिवार के इतिहास का एक छोटा-सा रिकॉर्ड छिपा है। कुछ जीन बालों और [[@skin-colour|त्वचा के रंग]] दोनों पर असर डालते हैं, पर बहुत-से अलग-अलग काम करते हैं। इसीलिए सोलोमन द्वीपों का कोई बच्चा एक साथ साँवली त्वचा और सुनहरे बालों वाला हो सकता है।

text: The German engineer Karl Benz is usually credited with building the first true car. In 1886 he received a patent for his Motorwagen, a three-wheeled carriage with a small petrol engine behind the seat. It had less power than a single horse and a top speed of around 16 km/h, about as fast as a child on a bicycle.

But it depends on what you count. In 1769, a French army engineer, Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot, built a heavy steam-powered tractor to haul cannons. And in the same year as Benz, Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach, also in [[@germany|Germany]], fitted a petrol engine to a four-wheeled carriage. Many people were racing toward the same idea.

sec.t:
Benz's machine looked like a large tricycle with spoked wheels. Its single-cylinder engine burned fuel inside a cylinder to push a [[piston|piston]], the basic idea still used in [[@cars-engine|petrol engines]] today. A belt and chains carried the power to the back wheels. There was no roof, no [[@accident-safety-glass|windscreen]] and only a simple [[lever|lever]] to steer.

Few people were interested at first. Horses were familiar, and the noisy machine scared some onlookers. Benz needed someone to prove it could be useful.

Around 1900, petrol cars were not winning yet. In the United States, steam, electric and petrol cars all competed. Electric cars were quiet and clean, and they didn't need to be cranked by hand to start. The US Department of Energy says around a third of cars on American roads at that time were electric.

But [[@batteries|batteries]] were heavy and needed long charging. Big oil finds in Texas made petrol cheap. And from 1912, petrol cars got electric starters, so nobody had to crank the engine. Electric cars faded, until they began to return in the 2000s.

In 1908, Henry Ford launched the Model T. In 1913 his factory in Michigan began using a [[@made-cars|moving assembly line]]. Instead of workers walking around a car, the car moved past them on a belt, and each worker did one small job. Building a car went from about 12 hours to about an hour and a half. Prices fell, and about 15 million Model Ts were sold.

[[@hist-first-car-india|Cars reached Indian cities]] in the early 1900s, owned mostly by the very rich, including [[@princely-states|maharajas]] who collected them. After independence, the Hindustan Ambassador, made near [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] from 1958 to 2014, became the car of politicians and taxi drivers. In 1983 the small, affordable Maruti 800 arrived, and for millions of families it was their first car.

Today engineers are working on cars that drive themselves, a story told in [[@self-driving|self-driving cars]].

text: Silicon Valley is the nickname for the area around the southern end of San Francisco Bay in California. It is famous because many of the world's biggest technology companies started or are based there, including Apple, Google, Meta, Intel and Nvidia.

The name comes from silicon, the material used to make computer [[@chips-silicon|chips]]. From the late 1950s, so many chip companies grew up in the area that a journalist, Don Hoefler, used the phrase "Silicon Valley USA" in a 1971 trade newspaper series. The name stuck, and the region became a symbol of new ideas, risky bets and enormous fortunes.

sec.t:
In 1956 William Shockley, a co-inventor of the [[transistor|transistor]], set up a company near Stanford to make silicon parts. He hired brilliant young scientists but was very hard to work for. In 1957 eight of them quit together and started their own company, Fairchild Semiconductor. Shockley reportedly called them traitors, and the nickname "the traitorous eight" stuck.

Fairchild was hugely successful. Many of its workers left to start companies of their own, and those workers' workers did the same. Two of the eight, Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore, founded Intel in 1968. Dozens of firms trace their roots back to Fairchild, a family tree that spread across the valley.

Silicon Valley also became the home of venture capital: investors who put money into young companies in return for a share. Many of their offices sit along one road, Sand Hill Road in Menlo Park. They expect most of their bets to fail, but one big success can pay for all the rest.

That attitude helps. In Silicon Valley, failing at a startup is often seen as experience rather than shame. Founders who fail can try again, and engineers move freely from one company to the next, carrying ideas with them.

The valley has drawn engineers from around the world. Many come from India, China, Taiwan and [[@vietnam|Vietnam]]. Indian Americans now lead some of the biggest companies there, and many Indian engineers return home to start companies in Bengaluru and [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]]. It's part of a much bigger story of the [[@indian-diaspora|Indian diaspora]], and of [[@sundar-ganges-tech|why so many tech leaders come from India]].

Success has costs. House prices in the valley are among the highest in the United States, so teachers, nurses and bus drivers often can't afford to live near their work. Traffic is heavy, and the gap between rich and poor is wide. Critics have also pointed out that tech companies there have hired too few women and too few Black and Latino workers.

Other places now copy the model. [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]] is often called "the Silicon Valley of India", and cities from Tel Aviv to Shenzhen compete for the same engineers. The fruit trees, meanwhile, are mostly gone, though a few orchards are kept as parks to remember the valley's sweeter past.

text: Simón Bolívar was a soldier and politician from Venezuela. In the early 1800s much of South America belonged to the Spanish Empire, ruled from far-off Madrid. Bolívar led armies that pushed Spain out of a huge stretch of the continent.

Six of today's countries owe their independence partly to him: Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia and Panama. Bolivia is even named after him. Across Latin America he is called *El Libertador*, the Liberator, and almost every town has a plaza or a statue in his honour.

sec.h: A rich boy who lost everything
sec.t:
Bolívar was born in Caracas in 1783 into one of the wealthiest families in the colony. By the age of nine he had lost both parents. A free-thinking tutor, Simón Rodríguez, filled his head with new ideas about liberty. His young wife died of fever less than a year after their wedding.

On a trip to Europe in 1805 he climbed the Monte Sacro hill in Rome with his old tutor. There, by his own later account, he swore not to rest until Spanish rule in America was broken. Back home, the chance came quickly. [[@napoleon|Napoleon]] had invaded Spain in 1808, and Spain's grip on its colonies was slipping.

sec.h: Defeat, exile and a second chance

sec.t:
In 1819 he tried something his enemies thought impossible. He marched his army across the plains during the rainy season, then up into the Andes, the longest mountain range above the sea on Earth. Soldiers from the hot lowlands climbed passes nearly 4,000 metres high in thin clothes. Many died of cold.

The survivors came down on the other side and took the Spanish by surprise. At the Battle of Boyacá on 7 August 1819 they won the victory that freed what is now Colombia. More wins followed, and by 1824 Spanish power in South America was almost gone.

sec.h: A hero with a hard side
sec.t:
Bolívar dreamed of one strong country, Gran Colombia, and even of a union of all the new nations. But regions quarrelled, and he grew more forceful. In 1828 he made himself dictator, and some of his old friends turned against him. That same year, plotters burst into his palace in Bogotá at night to kill him. His companion Manuela Sáenz, a fierce revolutionary from Ecuador, held them off while he escaped through a window. He later called her "the Liberator of the Liberator".

Gran Colombia broke apart, and Bolívar, ill and worn out, set off for exile. He died in Santa Marta, on the Colombian coast, in 1830, aged just 47. Two [[currency|currencies]] carry his name, Venezuela's bolívar and Bolivia's boliviano. In Lima, the capital of [[@peru|Peru]], a bronze Bolívar on horseback still faces the national Congress.

text: Tipu Sultan ruled the kingdom of Mysore, in today's Karnataka, from 1782 to 1799. He took over from his father, Hyder Ali, a soldier who had seized power in Mysore. Tipu was a fierce opponent of the British [[@east-india-company|East India Company]], and Mysore fought them in four wars, the first two led by his father and the last two by Tipu.

He is remembered for his iron-cased rockets, his interest in new technology and trade, and his attempts to ally with France against Britain. He died fighting at the walls of his capital, Srirangapatna, in 1799. Today he is one of the most argued-about figures in Indian history.

st.prompt: What was the case of a Mysore rocket made of?

Paper

st.reveal: Mysore rockets had iron tubes to hold the gunpowder, often tied to a long bamboo pole or blade. The strong iron case could hold more pressure than paper or cardboard, so the rockets flew farther, up to around two kilometres.

d.try: Make a balloon rocket. Thread a long string through a straw and tie it tight between two chairs. Blow up a balloon, hold it closed, tape it to the straw, then let go. The air rushing out backwards pushes the balloon forwards, the same idea behind every rocket.
myth: Tipu Sultan invented the rocket.
Rockets had been used in China and elsewhere for centuries. What made Mysore rockets special was their iron casing, which gave them more power and range than European rockets of the time.

sec.t:
Hyder Ali rose from a cavalry officer to become the real power in Mysore in the 1760s. His son Tipu, born in 1750 at Devanahalli near today's [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]], was trained in languages, religion and warfare from a young age.

Tipu fought beside his father against the British. In 1780, at the Battle of Pollilur near Kanchipuram, their forces crushed a British army. A Mysore rocket is thought to have blown up British ammunition carts during the battle. When Hyder Ali died in 1782, Tipu became ruler.

sec.h: A king who tried new things
sec.t:
Tipu was curious about technology and trade. He introduced a new calendar, new coins and new weights and measures. He set up trading posts abroad and encouraged silk farming in Mysore, which is still famous for its [[@silk|silk]] today.

He sent ambassadors to France and to the Ottoman Empire looking for allies against the British. In 1799 [[@napoleon|Napoleon]], then fighting in Egypt, wrote him a letter promising help. It never came in time.

His most famous possession is Tipu's Tiger, a life-size wooden tiger attacking a European soldier. Inside is a small organ, so that turning a handle makes the tiger growl and the man wail. It is now in the Victoria and Albert [[@museums|Museum]] in London.

The Third Anglo-Mysore War ended badly for Tipu in 1792. He lost about half his kingdom and had to send two young sons to the British as hostages until he paid a huge sum.

In 1799 the British, with their allies, attacked again. They besieged Srirangapatna, an island [[fortress|fortress]] in the Kaveri river. On 4 May 1799 they broke through the walls. Tipu was killed fighting near a gateway. His palace was looted, and many of his treasures were carried off to Britain.

sec.h: A ruler people still argue about
sec.t:
People still argue about Tipu. Many Indians see him as a brave patriot who died fighting [[colonial|colonial]] rule, an early hero of resistance. He gave grants to Hindu temples, and his letters to the Sringeri math, a Hindu [[monastery|monastery]], show respect.

Others point to evidence that his armies forced conversions and treated some communities very harshly, including Hindus in Kodagu and Malabar and Catholic Christians in Mangaluru. Historians argue over how much of this was religious and how much was the brutal warfare of the time. Both sides agree he was one of the toughest opponents the British met in India.

text: Nairobi is the capital of Kenya, in East Africa, and one of the strangest mixes of city and wild anywhere. On one side of a fence there are glass office towers, traffic jams and phone shops. On the other side, lions hunt zebras and buffaloes wallow in mud.

About 44 lakh people lived in the city at the 2019 [[census|census]], and more arrive every year. It sits about 1,795 m above sea level, higher than most hill stations in India, so it rarely gets very hot even though it is close to the [[equator|equator]]. It is a centre for business, technology, wildlife protection and the United Nations.

options.t: Cool water
Big lion
Red earth

st.reveal: The Maasai called a stream here Enkare Nairobi, "the place of cool water". Railway builders camped beside it in 1899, and the camp grew into a capital city.

myth: Africa is one hot country full of jungle, and its cities are small.
Africa has 54 countries. Nairobi is a large, modern city high on a plateau, where nights can be cool enough for a jumper and the land around it is mostly grassland, not jungle.

sec.t:
Nairobi National Park opened in 1946, the first national park in Kenya. It covers about 117 square kilometres, a little over half the area of Kolkata city, and its main gate is only about 7 km from the city centre.

Giraffes, zebras, lions, cheetahs, hippos and over 400 kinds of birds live there. It is also a [[sanctuary|sanctuary]] for black rhinos, which are critically [[endangered|endangered]]. Three sides of the park are fenced. The southern side stays open, so animals can wander out to the wider [[savanna|savanna]] and back during their yearly migrations.

In 1899, British engineers building a railway from Mombasa on the coast to Lake Victoria needed a base before the line climbed into steep hills. They chose a swampy spot by a cool stream. Workers from India made up much of the labour force, and many stayed. That is one reason Nairobi still has old Hindu temples, Sikh gurdwaras and families of Indian origin.

The camp grew fast. By 1907 it was the capital of British East Africa. When Kenya became independent in 1963, Nairobi stayed the capital.

The city grew in rings. The old centre has colonial-era buildings and the tall, round Kenyatta International Convention Centre. Around it spread neighbourhoods rich and poor. One of them is Kibera, among the largest informal settlements in Africa, where hundreds of thousands of people live in small homes of tin and mud brick.

{{story:wangari-maathai}}

In 1989, the government planned a 60-storey tower in Uhuru Park, one of Nairobi's few big green spaces. [[@wangari-maathai|Wangari Maathai]], a scientist who had started a tree-planting movement, protested loudly. She was mocked and even arrested at times, but the tower was never built.

Later she helped save Karura Forest on the city's northern edge from being cut up for housing. Today you can walk or cycle under its trees and find a waterfall. In 2004, Maathai became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

sec.h: The city that sends money by text
sec.t:
In 2007, a Kenyan phone company launched M-Pesa, a way to send money with a simple text message, even on a basic phone with no internet. A farmer could pay school fees, and a worker in the city could send cash to a grandmother in a village hundreds of kilometres away, in seconds.

It spread so fast that most Kenyan adults now use it. Tech companies opened offices in the city, and people started calling Nairobi the "Silicon Savannah". India's [[@upi-payments|UPI]] works differently, but it chases the same idea of money that moves as easily as a message.

sec.h: Orphan elephants and a UN headquarters
sec.t:
On the edge of the park, a charity raises baby elephants whose mothers died. Each morning visitors watch keepers feed them milk from giant bottles. Nearby, at the Giraffe Centre, you can feed rare Rothschild's giraffes from a raised platform, and they lick the food off your hand with tongues about 45 cm long.

Nairobi is also home to the headquarters of the UN Environment Programme. And far from the city, out in dry country to the north-east, Kenya runs a very different service: a [[@oddity-camel-library|library carried by camels]].

text: People love ghost stories because they let us feel fear while we are safe. Your heart beats faster, your skin prickles and your breath catches, yet you are tucked in bed or sitting by a campfire with friends.
That mix of danger and safety is a thrill, like a roller coaster for the mind. When the story ends, your body relaxes and you feel a rush of relief.

Ghost stories also bring people together. They are told in groups, often at night, and the shared shiver is part of the fun. And they ask big questions, about death and memory and the things we can't explain.

st.prompt: Researchers watched visitors in a haunted house attraction. Who enjoyed it most?

options.t: People who were scared a medium amount
People who were terrified the whole time
People who were hardly scared at all

st.reveal: The most fun came from a middle level of fear. Too little was boring and too much stopped being fun, a bit like how a swing is best when it goes high, but not too high.

n.certNote: Researchers agree that people enjoy fear when they feel safe, but they are still testing exactly why. Different scientists stress different reasons, from practice for real danger to simply sharing a thrill.

myth: Bhangarh Fort is officially recognised as a haunted place.

The Archaeological Survey of India's sign at Bhangarh bans entry between sunset and sunrise, a rule found at many protected ruins. The haunted reputation comes from local legends and from travel shows.

sec.t:
Ghost stories are among the oldest stories we have. Around 100 CE, the Roman writer Pliny the Younger wrote a letter about a house in Athens that nobody would live in. At night came the clank of chains and a thin, old ghost.

A philosopher named Athenodorus rented the house anyway, because it was cheap. When the ghost beckoned, he followed it to a spot in the courtyard. Workers dug there the next day and found old bones. Once the bones were buried properly, the haunting stopped. Many later ghost stories follow the same pattern: a restless spirit and a wrong put right.

India has a deep store of spooky tales. In [[@vikram-betal|Vikram and Betal]], a king must carry a corpse possessed by a ghost. Each time, Betal tells a story with a riddle at the end, and whenever the king answers, the ghost flies back to its tree.

Grandparents across India tell of bhoots with backward feet, of churails and of the brahmarakshas who haunts old trees. Bengali writers, including Satyajit Ray, wrote ghost stories for young readers. [[@ruskin-bond|Ruskin Bond]] set many of his in the misty hills around Mussoorie, where a ghost might be a lonely boy or a friendly old man.

sec.h: Your body on a scary story
sec.t:
When a story frightens you, a small part of your brain called the [[amygdala|amygdala]] raises the alarm. Your body releases [[adrenaline|adrenaline]]. Your heart speeds up and your muscles get ready to run, even though you are only listening.

But another part of your brain knows you are safe. So the [[@fear|fear]] never gets out of hand. Some scientists think this is useful practice, letting us try out scary feelings without real danger. At Aarhus University in Denmark, a team called the Recreational Fear Lab studies people at haunted house attractions to learn more.

It also explains why ghost stories work best in the dark. With less to see, your brain fills the gaps with guesses about what might be there, and when you are already on edge, those guesses tend to be scary ones. A coat on a hook becomes a figure. A creak becomes a footstep.

{{story:brain-works}}

Ghost stories often belong to the darkest, coldest time of year. In Victorian Britain, families told them at Christmas. [[@charles-dickens|Charles Dickens]] wrote A Christmas Carol in 1843, in which three spirits visit a mean old man named Scrooge and change him for good.

One Cambridge scholar, M. R. James, wrote new ghost stories and read them aloud to friends on Christmas Eve, by the light of a single candle.

In the USA, ghosts come out at [[@halloween|Halloween]], with haunted hayrides and costumes. In India, some families tell spooky tales on rainy [[monsoon|monsoon]] nights when the power goes out. In each case the weather outside makes the warm room feel safer, and the story feels scarier.

Do ghosts exist? There is no scientific evidence that they do. But the stories are real, and so is the shiver they give you.

text: Roald Dahl was a British writer who lived from 1916 to 1990. His children's books, including Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, [[@matilda|Matilda]], The BFG, The Witches and Fantastic Mr Fox, have sold many millions of copies and been translated into dozens of languages.

His stories are popular because they take children's side. Grown-ups in Dahl's books are often greedy, cruel or ridiculous, and clever children beat them. The stories are funny and a little bit gross, full of made-up words and nasty surprises. Readers feel the writer is a naughty friend who knows exactly what bores them.

A type of dream

st.reveal: The snozzcumber is the only vegetable that grows in Giant Country, and it tastes revolting. Dahl invented hundreds of words like it. He called the BFG's language gobblefunk.

He first became famous for spooky, twisty short stories for adults. He also wrote film scripts, including the James Bond film You Only Live Twice and Chitty Chitty Bang Bang.

sec.t:
When the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]] began, Dahl joined the Royal Air Force as a fighter pilot. In 1940 his plane crash-landed in the Libyan desert, and he was badly hurt. He recovered and flew again in Greece, before headaches forced him to stop.

He was then sent to Washington, D.C., to work at the British Embassy. There he also passed information to British intelligence, and he began writing about his flying adventures. His first book for children, The Gremlins (1943), was about tiny creatures said to sabotage aircraft, an idea RAF pilots joked about.

Dahl's books share a few tricks. Characters get the punishments they deserve, often in spectacular ways: Augustus Gloop is sucked up a chocolate pipe. Children are brave and clever, like Matilda, who teaches herself to read at three. And the language is a feast.

The BFG speaks gobblefunk, full of words like "whizzpopper" and "snozzcumber". Dahl also loved rhymes and nonsense poems. In 2016, the hundredth anniversary of his birth, the Oxford English Dictionary added several words connected with his books. That shows how [[@dictionaries|dictionaries]] follow the words people actually use.

From 1978, most of his children's books were illustrated by Quentin Blake. His scratchy, lively drawings fit Dahl's stories so well that many readers can't picture one without the other.

Dahl's life had sadness in it. His daughter Olivia died of measles in 1962, aged seven, and he later urged parents to vaccinate their children. He also helped invent a medical valve after his baby son was injured in an accident.

He also said hurtful things. In interviews he made antisemitic remarks, attacking Jewish people. In 2020 his family publicly apologised for them. In 2023 his publisher changed some words in new editions, which caused a big argument about whether old books should be edited. The publisher then decided to keep the original versions in print too.

His birthday, 13 September, is celebrated as Roald Dahl Day in many schools. A museum about his life opened in 2005 in Great Missenden, the English village where he lived and [[@how-to-write-story|wrote in a hut]] at the bottom of his garden.

text: Gujarati cooks like to balance tastes. A spoonful of jaggery or sugar often goes into dal, kadhi and vegetables, along with lemon, [[@tamarind|tamarind]] or kokum for sourness, green chillies for heat, and salt. The result is food that tastes sweet, sour, spicy and salty at the same time.

Nobody knows for sure why this habit began. Many people link it to the hot, dry [[climate|climate]] and to salty water and soil in parts of the state, which made food taste salty. Gujarat also has many vegetarian families, and a little sweetness may have helped make simple [[@lentils-world|lentils]] and vegetables more filling and tasty.

st.prompt: Why does dhokla turn out so soft and full of tiny holes?

options.t: Gas bubbles from fermentation or a raising agent puff up the batter
It is whipped with a fork for an hour
The steam pushes holes into it from below

st.reveal: Traditional dhokla batter is left to ferment, so microbes make gas bubbles. Quick versions use a raising agent like fruit salt instead. Steaming sets the bubbles, leaving a soft, spongy cake.

sec.t:
Gujarat has one of India's largest vegetarian populations. [[@jain-agamas|Jainism]], a religion that teaches non-violence towards all living things, has deep roots there. Many Jains follow the teachings of [[@mahavira|Mahavira]] and avoid meat and also root vegetables such as onions, garlic and potatoes, because pulling them up harms tiny creatures in the soil.

Many Hindu Vaishnav families in Gujarat are vegetarian too. So Gujarati cooks became experts at making lentils, gram flour, vegetables and milk exciting.

Gujarat is famous for its snacks, known as farsan. Dhokla is a steamed, spongy cake made from fermented rice and lentil batter or gram flour. Khandvi is thin rolls of cooked gram flour batter, topped with mustard seeds and coconut. Thepla is a soft flatbread with fenugreek leaves that stays fresh for days.

On Dussehra, Gujaratis eat huge amounts of fafda, crunchy gram flour strips, with sweet [[@food-jalebi|jalebi]]. Gujarat even has its own kind of snack shop, the farsan mart, selling dozens of kinds of namkeen.

A full Gujarati thali can be enormous. It might include dal, kadhi, two or three vegetables, rotli (thin rotis), rice, farsan, [[@pickles-achar|pickles]], chutneys and a sweet like shrikhand, sweetened strained yogurt. Servers keep refilling your plate until you firmly say no.

In winter, families cook undhiyu, a mix of beans, purple yam, small brinjals, potatoes and fenugreek dumplings. The name comes from "undhu", meaning upside down, because it was traditionally cooked in clay pots placed upside down in a pit with fire on top.

Gujarat has several distinct regional styles. Surat is famous for its love of food and for dishes like locho, a soft steamed snack. Kathiyawadi food from the Saurashtra [[peninsula|peninsula]] is spicier, with garlic chutney, millet rotlas and [[@lassi-chaas|buttermilk]]. Kutch, near the desert, cooks with bajra and dairy.

Gujaratis have also carried their food around the world. In parts of New Jersey, London and East Africa, you can buy fresh dhokla and thepla from shops run by Gujarati families.
